'''William Earl Bergey''' (February 9, 1945 – December 25, 2024) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[linebacker]] who played for 12 seasons, most notably with the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] of the [[American Football League]] (AFL) in the [[1969 NFL/AFL draft]], the year before the [[AFL–NFL merger]] was completed and continued to play with the Bengals in the NFL until 1973. Bergey signed with the Eagles the following year, where he played seven seasons until retiring in 1981.

During his career, Bergey received five [[Pro Bowl]] and two first-team [[All-Pro]] selections and made an appearance in [[Super Bowl XV]], his final professional game. He is an inductee of the [[Philadelphia Eagles#Eagles Hall of Fame|Eagles Hall of Fame]] and the [[Philadelphia Sports Hall of Fame]].

==Early life and education==
Bergey was born in [[South Dayton, New York]], on February 9, 1945.<ref name="AP-Obit" /> He graduated from Pine Valley Central High School in South Dayton in 1964, and graduated from [[Arkansas State University]] (ASU), where he played under coach [[Bennie Ellender|Bernie Ellender]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Demirel |first=Evin |date=2020-07-29 |title=Bill Bergey, A-State's Greatest Player, Admits He Suffered In Jonesboro |url=https://www.bestofarkansassports.com/bill-bergey-a-states-greatest-player-admits-he-suffered-in-jonesboro/ |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=Best of Arkansas Sports |language=en-US}}</ref> He was an [[1968 Little All-America college football team|All-American]] for the [[Arkansas State Red Wolves football|Arkansas State Indians]] (now [[Arkansas State Red Wolves|Red Wolves]]) and has since been voted by fans the Top Player in Arkansas State history.<ref name="Bill Bergey">{{cite web|url=http://www.chautauquasportshalloffame.org/billbergey.php|title =Bill Bergey| publisher=Chautauqua Sports Hall of Fame|access-date= June 16, 2013}}</ref> He was a charter member of Delta Eta chapter of [[Kappa Alpha Order]] at ASU.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Notable KAs |url=https://www.kappaalphaorder.org/about/history/notable-kas/ |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=Kappa Alpha Order |language=en-US}}</ref> He graduated in 1969 with a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in [[physical education]], and a commission in the [[Army Reserves]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Bill Bergey (1982) – Hall of Honor |url=https://astateredwolves.com/honors/hall-of-honor/bill-bergey/1 |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=Arkansas State University |language=en}}</ref>

Originally positioned at offensive lineman and noseguard, he was moved to linebacker in 1966.<ref name=":0" /> At ASU, Bergey set records for best tackling average in a season, most fumble recoveries in a season, most tackles in a game, most tackles in a season, and most career tackles.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" /> He once had 33 tackles in a single game, and averaged 19.6 tackles per game in 1968.<ref name=":0" />

He played in three post-season all-star games during his ASU career (the [[Senior Bowl]], the North–South Game, and one of the last [[Chicago Charities College All-Star Game|Chicago All-Star Games]], against the New York Jets<ref name=":3" />). Bergey was selected to the [[Southland Conference|All-Southland Conference]] team three times and to the Southland Conference All-First Decade Team. Bergey's jersey number 66 was retired by ASU, and he was the first person to go up on its Wall of Fame.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://kasu.astate.edu/herald/archive/sports/1118football.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100621114322/http://www.kasu.astate.edu/herald/archive/sports/1118football.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 21, 2010 |title=ASU to retire number Saturday at football game |publisher=The Herald Archives |access-date=June 16, 2013 }}</ref><ref name=":0" /> He was inducted into ASU's Hall of Honor in 1982.<ref name=":1" /> Despite the accolades, Bergey's southern schoolmates would physically fight with the "Yankee" from Western New York, and his actual time at ASU in [[Jonesboro, Arkansas|Jonesboro]] was difficult.<ref name=":0" />

==Professional career==
===Cincinnati Bengals===
Bergey was drafted by the [[American Football League]]'s [[Cincinnati Bengals]] in the second round of the [[1969 NFL/AFL draft]], the 31st overall selection.<ref name=":5" />  He was chosen as an [[American Football League All-Star game|AFL All-Star]] in his rookie year, for the game held on January 17, 1970.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Tobias |first=Todd |title=1970 AFL All-Star Game Rosters |url=https://talesfromtheamericanfootballleague.com/488-2/1970-afl-all-star-game-rosters/ |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=Tales from the AFL |language=en-US}}</ref> He had two interceptions for the Bengals in his rookie year.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=Bill Bergey Pro Football Stats, Position, College, Transactions |url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/players/b/berg00800.html |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=www.profootballarchives.com}}</ref> For his efforts as a rookie, he was named the AFL Defensive Rookie of the Year by the [[Associated Press]], the final selections made for the AFL as a league prior to the merger.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/awards/awards_1969.htm | title=1969 Awards Voting | website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=BERGEBIL01 |title=Bill Bergey |publisher=databaseFootball.com |access-date=June 5, 2013 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130408102912/http://databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=BergeBil01 |archive-date=April 8, 2013 }}</ref><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Gehman |first=Jim |date=May 27, 2015 |title=Where Are They Now? LB Bill Bergey |url=https://www.philadelphiaeagles.com/news/where-are-they-now-lb-bill-bergey-15330191#:~:text=Making%20his%20home%20in%20suburban%20Philadelphia,%20Bergey%20is,a%20widely%20popular%20alumni%20representative%20for%20the%20Eagles. |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=www.philadelphiaeagles.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

Bergey played under Hall of Fame coach [[Paul Brown]] at Cincinnati.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=2013-10-04 |title=Where Are They Now: Bill Bergey |url=https://www.nationalfootballpost.com/2008-2018-nfp-archive/football-history/where-are-they-now-bill-bergey/ |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=National Football Post |language=en-CA}}</ref> He recorded three interceptions in the 1970 season,<ref name=":5" /> the first year for the team in the NFL. The Bengals made the postseason that year, losing to the [[Baltimore Colts]] in the divisional round 17–0,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Divisional Round – Cincinnati Bengals at Baltimore Colts – December 26th, 1970 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197012260clt.htm |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> but Bergey did not record a statistic. He recorded a fumble recovery to go with an unofficial "sack". He recorded an interception in his next two combined seasons (1971–1972). In his final season with Cincinnati in 1973, he had three interceptions and recovered three fumbles.<ref name=":5" />

===Florida Blazers and trade to Philadelphia Eagles===
Bergey signed a personal service contract on April 17, 1974, with the Washington Capitols, the owner of the [[World Football League]] (WFL)'s [[San Antonio Wings|Virginia Ambassadors]], which would later become the [[Florida Blazers]] once the circuit began play in July of that year. He was to have joined the WFL team in May 1976, after his contract with the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] expired following the 1975 season. However, the Bengals filed suit against Bergey for [[breach of contract]] and a [[injunction|temporary restraining order]] against the WFL and its franchises two days later on April 19. In the [[Hearing (law)|hearing]], which began on April 29 and was adjudicated 15 days later on May 14, the court concluded that Bergey had not breached his contract and the Bengals' motion for a temporary injunction was denied.<ref>[https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/FSupp/453/129/1487835/ ''Cincinnati Bengals, Inc. v. Bergey, 453 F. Supp. 129 (S.D. Ohio 1974)'' – Justia.com.] Retrieved November 26, 2020</ref><ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/1974/04/20/archives/bengals-get-writ-halting-wfl-raids-bengals-granted-order-barring.html "Bengals Get Writ Halting WFL Raids," Associated Press (AP), Friday, April 19, 1974.] Retrieved November 26, 2020</ref>

Bergey did not receive compensation from the Blazers and was released from his WFL contract.<ref>{{cite news |title=Bergey Sent By Bengals To Eagles |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1974/07/11/archives/bergey-sent-by-bengals-to-eagles.html |access-date=31 December 2024 |work=[[The New York Times]] |agency=Associated Press |date=July 11, 1974 |quote=The trade silenced a squabble between the Bengals and Bergey, a 6‐foot‐3‐inch, 243‐pound middle linebacker, over his jump to the W.F.L.'s Florida Blazers, effective with the 1976 season. Coach Paul Brown said Bergey went to the Eagles 'with no strings attached. Bill had not received his July 1 bonus payment from the W.F.L. Orlando team, and Orlando was willing to release its contract with Bergey.'}}</ref> He was traded from the Bengals to the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] for a [[1977 NFL draft|1977]] first-round selection, [[Wilson Whitley]], and first- and second-round picks in [[1978 NFL draft|1978]], [[Ross Browner]] and [[Ray Griffin]] respectively, on July 10, 1974.<ref>{{cite web |title=The 10 biggest trades in Eagles history |url=https://www.nbcsportsphiladelphia.com/nfl/philadelphia-eagles/the-10-biggest-trades-in-eagles-history/178180/ |website=NBC Sports Philadelphia |access-date=31 December 2024 |date=17 February 2021 |quote=July 10, 1974: The Eagles traded a 1st-round pick in 1976 and 1st- and 2nd-round picks in 1977 to the Bengals for Bill Bergey: Bergey became a 1st-team all-pro in his first year with the Eagles and made the Pro Bowl in each of his first five years here. He retired after the 1980 Super Bowl season and is now in the Eagles Hall of Fame. The Bengals used the picks they got from the Eagles to select Wilson Whitley, Ross Browner and Ray Griffin.}}</ref>

In July 1974, Bergey signed a five-year contract with the Eagles.<ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/1974/07/11/archives/bergey-sent-by-bengals-to-eagles.html "Bergey Sent By Bengals To Eagles," Associated Press (AP), Wednesday, July 10, 1974.] Retrieved November 26, 2020</ref><ref>[https://prosportstransactions.com/football/DraftTrades/Years/1977.htm 1977 NFL Draft Pick Transactions, May 3 (Rounds 1–5) & 4 (Rounds 6–12) – Pro Sports Transactions.] Retrieved November 26, 2020</ref> The Blazers ceased operating following the 1974 season, and the WFL itself ceased business in 1975.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=KNZVAAAAIBAJ&pg=6366%2C6777086 |work=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon |agency=Associated Press |title='It's over' for WFL |date=October 22, 1975 |page=1E}}</ref>

===Philadelphia Eagles===
Bergey played a key role in the Eagles' subsequent rise, culminating in the trip to [[Super Bowl XV]]. With the Eagles, Bergey, a four-time Pro Bowl selection as an Eagle (1974, 1976–1978),<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=Mullin |first=Matt |date=April 23, 2015 |title=Is Bill Bergey the greatest living Eagle? |url=https://www.phillyvoice.com/who-greatest-living-eagle-bill-bergey/ |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=PhillyVoice |language=english}}</ref> set the NFL record for most [[interception]]s by a [[linebacker]] and became the highest-paid defensive player in the league with a four-year contract for $1 million.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.astate.edu/a/military-science/hall-of-heroes/bill-bergey/index.dot|title=BILL BERGEY All-Pro NFL Football Player|publisher=Arkansas State University|access-date=June 16, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150906052724/http://www.astate.edu/a/military-science/hall-of-heroes/bill-bergey/index.dot|archive-date=September 6, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> He earned Eagles MVP status three times from the votes of his teammates.<ref name=":2" /> In his first year with the Eagles, Bergey was runner up to [[Joe Greene|"Mean" Joe Greene]] for defensive player of the year.<ref name=":3" />

Bergey played 91 games as an Eagle, and started every game in six of the seven years in Philadelphia, with 18 interceptions and 15 fumble recoveries.<ref name=":6" /> Bergey recorded 233 tackles in a single season with the Eagles, and once held the league record for interceptions by a linebacker with five.<ref>{{Cite web |title=HALL OF VERY GOOD – 2012 – PFRA {{!}} PROFESSIONAL FOOTBALL RESEARCHERS ASSOCIATION |url=https://www.profootballresearchers.org/hall-of-very-good-2012.html |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=www.profootballresearchers.org}}</ref> He was a popular player who was the foundation of the "Gang Green" defense<ref name=":0" /> that brought the Eagles back to the playoffs in 1978, 1979 and 1980. They went all the way to the [[Super Bowl XV|Super Bowl in 1981]] after winning the [[1980–81 NFL playoffs|NFC championship game]] against the [[Dallas Cowboys]] 20–7 in the 1980 season.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Philadelphia Eagles Team History |url=https://www.statmuse.com/nfl/team/philadelphia-eagles-49/history |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=StatMuse |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://articles.philly.com/1993-12-29/sports/25940132_1_fire-scene-keith-krepfle-eagles|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130620030815/http://articles.philly.com/1993-12-29/sports/25940132_1_fire-scene-keith-krepfle-eagles|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 20, 2013|title =Bergey: House Fire 'Devastating'| publisher=Philly.Com|access-date= June 16, 2013}}</ref> He suffered a serious knee injury in 1979. He returned in 1980, but it would be Bergey's last season. His ability level was reduced by the injury (he evaluated it at 65%), and he could no longer reach runners in time to make the play; but he was still named All NFC by the ''[[The Sporting News|Sporting News]]'' and went to the Super Bowl.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":6" />

Bergey played 159 games and recorded nearly 1,200 tackles.<ref name=":2" /> He was first- or second-team All Pro/All NFL or All-NFC from 1974 to 1978 ([[1974 All-Pro Team]], [[1975 All-Pro Team]], [[1976 All-Pro Team]], [[1977 All-Pro Team]], [[1978 All-Pro Team]]).<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |date=2012-07-25 |title=Bill Bergey – Greater Buffalo Sports Hall of Fame |url=https://www.buffalosportshallfame.com/bill-bergey/ |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=www.buffalosportshallfame.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":5" /> He finished his career with 27 interceptions that he returned for 397 yards, 16 unofficial sacks (beginning in 1970), and 21 fumble recoveries.<ref name=":5" />

Bergey had conflicts with guard [[Conrad Dobler]] of the Eagles' [[NFC East]] rival [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]], who once spit on him while he was downed and injured.<ref name=page2>
{{cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/page2/s/list/dirtiest/players.html |website=[[ESPN.com]] |title=Dirtiest Professional Team Players | access-date=December 10, 2017}}</ref> His and Dobler's volatile relationship was ranked by [[NFL Films]] at No. 9 on the [[NFL Top 10]] list of feuds.<ref name="TopFeuds">{{cite web |title=Top 10 feuds in NFL history |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/top-10-feuds-in-nfl-history-09000d5d80873de6 |website=[[NFL.com]] |access-date=August 20, 2022 |date=May 27, 2008}}</ref>

Bergey retired from professional football in 1981, his last game being Super Bowl XV.<ref name=":6" /> He was inducted into the Eagles Roll of Honor in 1988 with [[Tommy McDonald (American football)|Tommy McDonald]].<ref name="Bill Bergey"/><ref name=":2" /> In 2012, the [[Professional Football Researchers Association]] named Bergey to the PFRA Hall of Very Good Class of 2012.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.profootballresearchers.com/hall-of-very-good-2012.htm |title=Hall of Very Good Class of 2012. |access-date=November 21, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160913215154/http://profootballresearchers.com/hall-of-very-good-2012.htm |archive-date=September 13, 2016 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He is considered one of the top Eagles of all time.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fitzpatrick |first=Frank |date=2022-09-10 |title=The 50 greatest Eagles players of all time |url=https://www.inquirer.com/eagles/a/eagles-best-players-ranking-all-time-20220910.html |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=Inquirer.com |language=en}}</ref> He was inducted into the [[Philadelphia Sports Hall of Fame]] in 2011.<ref>{{Cite web |author=<!--Not stated-->|date=2012-07-08 |title=Philadelphia Sports Hall of Fame inductees |url=https://www.inquirer.com/philly/sports/sportsweek/20120708_List_of_inductees__Philadelphia_Sports_Hall_of_Fame.html |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=inquirer.com |language=en}}</ref> The same year, the [[Philadelphia Sports Writers Association]] recognized Bergey with its Living Legend Award.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2011-02-01 |title=Philadelphia Sports Writers Association Awards |url=https://www.inquirer.com/philly/sports/20110201_Philadelphia_Sports_Writers_Association_Awards.html |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=inquirer.com |language=en}}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
During his playing days, Bergey served as a lieutenant in the [[National Guard (United States)|U.S. Army Reserve]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=McPherson |first=Chris |date=December 25, 2024 |title= Eagles mourn the passing of Bill Bergey, NFC Champion and member of the franchise's Hall of Fame  |url=https://www.philadelphiaeagles.com/news/eagles-mourn-the-passing-of-bill-bergey |access-date=December 27, 2024 |website=Philadelphia Eagles}}</ref>

Bergey served as a [[color commentator]] on radio broadcasts of the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] from 1982 to 1983. He also provided pre-game and post-game radio and television commentary for the team during the season for over 20 years.<ref name=":6" />

Bergey was a plaintiff in the concussion related lawsuit against the NFL filed and settled in a Philadelphia federal court.<ref>{{Cite web |author1=John P. Martin |author2=Frank Fitzpatrick |date=2013-08-31 |title=Prospect of long trial helped drive NFL settlement |url=https://www.inquirer.com/philly/news/homepage/20130901_Prospect_of_long_trial_helped_drive_NFL_settlement.html |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=inquirer.com |language=en}}</ref>

Bergey later lived in [[Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania]] with his wife Micky Kay. He had three sons and multiple grandchildren.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> He is a member of the Greater Buffalo Sports Hall of Fame (2004).<ref name=":4" /> In 1989, he became a member of the [[Chautauqua County, New York|Chautauqua]] Sports Hall of Fame.<ref name=":3" />

His son [[Jake Bergey]] is a retired [[box lacrosse|lacrosse]] player for the [[Philadelphia Wings]] of the [[National Lacrosse League]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Murrow |first=John |date=2014-02-10 |title=Wings retire Jake Bergey's number |url=https://www.inquirer.com/philly/sports/wings/20140210_Wings_retire_Jake_Bergey_s_number.html |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=inquirer.com |language=en}}</ref> and his son Josh Bergey is a retired lacrosse player for the [[Chesapeake Bayhawks]] of the [[Major League Lacrosse]].<ref>{{cite web|url= http://articles.philly.com/2005-05-07/sports/25439496_1_lacrosse-coach-josh-bergey-jake-bergey|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140319151128/http://articles.philly.com/2005-05-07/sports/25439496_1_lacrosse-coach-josh-bergey-jake-bergey|url-status= dead|archive-date= March 19, 2014|title = Josh Bergey enjoying life on sidelines Marple Newtown rookie lacrosse coach says the Tigers are on their way to contending.| publisher= Philly.com|access-date= June 5, 2013}}</ref> Bill's brother [[Bruce Bergey]] was a standout player for the [[Portland Thunder (WFL)|Portland Storm]] of the WFL.<ref>{{Cite web |title=World Football League |url=http://wfl.charlottehornetswfl.com/rosters_1974/portland_storm.php |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=wfl.charlottehornetswfl.com}}</ref>

In the film ''[[Silver Linings Playbook]]'', [[Robert De Niro]]'s character Pat Solitano Sr., an Eagles fanatic, wears a number 66 Bill Bergey jersey.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Carchidi |first=Sam |date=2012-11-14 |title=Eagles star in Silver Linings Playbook |url=https://www.inquirer.com/philly/sports/eagles/20121114_Eagles_star_in_Silver_Linings_Playbook.html |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=inquirer.com |language=en}}</ref>

Bergey was diagnosed with oral cancer in 2021 and determinedly fought in response to the disease, finding encouragement and inspiration from others, including former Buffalo Bills quarterback [[Jim Kelly]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bill Bergey opens up about his battle with cancer |url=https://www.philadelphiaeagles.com/news/bill-bergey-cancer-battle-crucial-catch-commanders-eagles |access-date=2024-10-29 |publisher=Philadelphia Eagles |language=en-US}}</ref>

In October 2024, Bergey was among 60 former players under consideration for the 2025 Pro Football Hall of Fame class in the Senior category,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-10-03 |title=Five With Eagles' Ties Make The Cut To 50 In Hall Of Fame' Seniors Category |url=https://www.si.com/nfl/eagles/news/five-with-eagles-ties-make-the-cut-to-50-in-hall-of-fame-seniors-category-01j9a3zwx2kv |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=Philadelphia Eagles On SI |language=en-US}}</ref> though he did not make it to the next round of 31 candidates.<ref>{{Cite web |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=2024-10-22 |title=One former Bengals player makes next cut in Pro Football Hall of Fame seniors division |url=https://local12.com/sports/bengals/one-former-bengals-player-makes-next-cut-pro-football-hall-of-fame-seniors-division-cincinnati-ken-anderson-isaac-curtis-lemar-parrish-bill-bergey-nfl |access-date=2024-10-29 |website=WKRC |language=en}}</ref>

Bergey died from cancer in Chadds Ford on December 25, 2024. He was 79.<ref name="AP-Obit">{{cite news |last1=Gelston |first1=Dan |title=Bill Bergey, a Pro Bowl linebacker for the Eagles, dies at 79 |url=https://apnews.com/article/bill-bergey-dead-philadelphia-eagles-924d74fb5e364b7a23e96b5b103fbb92 |access-date=31 December 2024 |publisher=AP News |date=25 December 2024 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Former Philadelphia Eagles linebacker, and long-time WDEL guest, Bill Bergey has died, according to his family. |url=https://www.wdel.com/news/legendary-philadelphia-eagle-and-frequent-wdel-guest-bill-bergey-dies/article_eb532708-c2ce-11ef-8ed8-772284547e73.html |access-date=25 December 2024 |publisher=WDEL |date=25 December 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Brennan |first1=Shane |title=Eagles legend Bill Bergey dies at 79 |url=https://eu.delawareonline.com/story/news/local/2024/12/25/eagles-legend-bergey-dies-at-79/77213063007/ |access-date=25 December 2024 |publisher=Delaware Online |date=25 December 2024}}</ref>

'''William Timothy Callahan''' (born April 11, 1964) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive back]] for the [[Buffalo Bills]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Pittsburgh Panthers football|Pittsburgh Panthers]] while at the [[University of Pittsburgh]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/C/CallBi20.htm |title=Bill Callahan Stats |publisher=Pro-Football-Reference.com |access-date=April 11, 2023}}</ref>

Callahan switched from a [[running back]] to his best known position as a defensive back in 1983, after a suggestion from his coach Joe Naunchik, although many did not initially understand his choice to change position. Callahan became the starting favourite in that position after his predecessor Ray Weatherspoon was dropped following an altercation.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-pittsburgh-press |title=Callahan: Safety Valve For Panthers |newspaper=The Pittsburgh Press |page=146 |date=August 21, 1983}}</ref>

In [[1986 NFL draft|1986]], he was favourably compared to [[Tom Flynn (American football)|Tom Flynn]] and was described by ''[[The Pittsburgh Press]]'' as being "one of the brightest young safeties in the NFL". He was recorded as running the {{convert|40|yard}}-dash in 4.48 seconds, making him among the fastest safeties playing at that time. His time was comparable to then top-rated safety [[Craig Swoope]], who did the same run in 4.57 seconds.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/122965489/the-pittsburgh-press/ |title=Callahan is timing things just right for NFL draft |newspaper=The Pittsburgh Press |page=151 |date=April 27, 1986}}</ref>

Head coach | highlights = * [[List of Super Bowl champions|Super Bowl champion]] ([[Super Bowl XL|XL]]) * [[NFL Coach of the Year Award#AP NFL Coach of the Year|AP NFL Coach of the Year]] (1992) * 2× [[NFL Coach of the Year Award#Sporting News NFL Coach of the Year|Sporting News NFL Coach of the Year]] (1992, 2004) * Best Coach/Manager [[ESPY Award]] (2006) * [[Pittsburgh Steelers#Hall of Honor|Pittsburgh Steelers Hall of Honor]] * [[Pittsburgh Pro Football Hall of Fame]] | statlabel1 = Games played | statvalue1 = 45 | statlabel2 = Games started | statvalue2 = 4 | statlabel3 = Fumble recoveries | statvalue3 = 1 | regular_record = {{Winning percentage|149|90|1|record=y}} | playoff_record = {{Winning percentage|12|9|record=y}} | overall_record = {{Winning percentage|161|99|1|record=y}} | pfrcoach = CowhBi0 | HOF = bill-cowher }} '''William Laird Cowher''' ({{IPAc-en|'|k|aʊ|.|ər}}; born May 8, 1957) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[linebacker]] and coach who served as the [[head coach]] for the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 15 seasons. He began his coaching career as an assistant under [[Marty Schottenheimer]] for the [[Cleveland Browns]] and [[Kansas City Chiefs]], serving as the latter's defensive coordinator from 1989 to 1991. In 1992, Cowher was named head coach of the Steelers, a position he held until his retirement following the 2006 season. After retiring, Cowher joined ''[[The NFL Today]]'' as a studio analyst. Under Cowher, the Steelers won eight division titles, two [[AFC Championship Game]]s, and [[Super Bowl XL]]. Cowher's Super Bowl victory marked the first championship title for the franchise in over two decades and the first not to be won by [[Chuck Noll]], his predecessor. The Steelers appeared in the postseason 10 times with Cowher, including six consecutive appearances from his 1992 hiring to 1997, which made him the second NFL head coach to reach the playoffs during each of his first six seasons after [[Paul Brown]]. Cowher was inducted to the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2020. ==Early life and college== Cowher was born and raised in [[Crafton, Pennsylvania]], a suburb of [[Pittsburgh]]. Growing up, he lived only about {{convert|5|miles}} from [[Three Rivers Stadium]].{{Cite web |last=Rodgers |first=Tarrian |date=July 14, 2021 |title=Bill Cowher: The Hall of Fame ScowlUp to date sports, film and entertainment news |url=https://www.newsstitchedmedia.com/post/bill-cowher-the-hall-of-fame-scowl |access-date=November 8, 2024 |website=News Stitched Media |language=en}} Cowher is the son of the late Laird and Dorothy Cowher. His father attended [[Duquesne University]] in Pittsburgh's [[Bluff (Pittsburgh)|Bluff]] neighborhood,{{Cite web|url=https://triblive.com/sports/steelers/bill-cowher-speaks-to-duquesne-graduates-accepts-honorary-doctorate/|title=Bill Cowher talks leadership, Steelers draft, Pickett at Duquesne graduation as he receives honorary degree|first=Paul|last=Guggenheimer|date=May 5, 2023|website=TribLIVE.com}} where he was briefly a classmate with eventual Steelers owner [[Dan Rooney]].{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pNOkc67Jqlg |title=Big Ben & Coach Cowher talk 2004 draft, SB XL, getting Jerome Bettis to return and more! Ep. 27 |date=May 8, 2023 |last=Channel Seven |access-date=November 8, 2024 |via=YouTube}} Cowher has two brothers, Dale and Doug.{{Cite web|url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/legacyremembers/laird-cowher-obituary?id=22576064|title=LAIRD COWHER Obituary (2010) - Legacy Remembers|website=Legacy.com}} The Cowher family resided on Hawthorne Avenue, in Crafton, while Cowher grew up.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/01/23/sports/football/cowher-feels-a-void-in-pittsburgh.html|title=Cowher Feels a Void in Pittsburgh|first=Lee|last=Jenkins|work=The New York Times |date=January 23, 2005|via=NYTimes.com}} [[File:Cowher1975.jpg|thumb|left|190px|Cowher in 1975]] While attending [[Carlynton School District|Carlynton High School]], Cowher excelled in football, basketball, and track. As a senior, he was named "Most Athletic" and captain of the Cougars football team.{{cite web |last=Keane |first=Jennifer E. |date=2007 |title=Bill Cowher |url=https://pabook.libraries.psu.edu/literary-cultural-heritage-map-pa/bios/cowher__bill |website=www.pabook.libraries.psu.edu |access-date=December 14, 2025}} Despite his efforts on the field, Cowher was not offered many scholarships as a football player due to being deemed "undersized" for the linebacker position.{{Cite web|url=https://www.fayobserver.com/story/sports/college/acc/2023/09/29/nc-state-football-bill-cowher-nfl-pittsburgh-steelers/71008065007/|title=How NC State football 'forged' Hall of Fame NFL coach Bill Cowher|first=Rodd|last=Baxley|date=September 29, 2023|website=The Fayetteville Observer}} When Cowher graduated in 1975, he committed to [[North Carolina State University]], one of the few schools that offered him a scholarship. During his time at NC State, Cowher was a three-year starting linebacker for the Wolfpack. He currently owns the school record for most tackles in a single season with 195.{{Cite web |last=Peeler |first=Tim |date=September 27, 2023 |title=Athletics To Honor 2 NC State Legends |url=https://news.ncsu.edu/2023/09/athletics-to-honor-2-nc-state-legends/ |access-date=June 1, 2025 |website=NC State News}} As a senior, Cowher was voted to be a team captain and was named the team's Most Valuable Player (MVP). He graduated from NC State in 1979, receiving a [[bachelor's degree]] in education while also preparing for the 1979 NFL Draft.{{Cite web|url=https://pabook.libraries.psu.edu/literary-cultural-heritage-map-pa/bios/Cowher__Bill|title=Pennsylvania Center for the Book|website=pabook.libraries.psu.edu}} Cowher's college performance was motivated by making games “personal”. He would often re-read his rejection letters from schools he would play against. Cowher's strategy of playing angry and internalizing personal connections against his opponents would later influence his aggressive coaching style. Cowher once compared himself to [[Freddy Krueger]], stating that he wanted to be his opponents' "worst nightmare".{{cite video |title=Big Ben & Coach Cowher talk 2004 draft, SB XL, getting Jerome Bettis to return and more! Ep. 27 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pNOkc67Jqlg |author=Channel Seven |date=May 8, 2023 |access-date=October 30, 2024 |time=20:56}} ==Professional career== Cowher went undrafted in the [[1979 NFL draft]]. He began his NFL career as a linebacker with the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] in 1979, but signed with the [[Cleveland Browns]] the following year. Cowher played three seasons from 1980 to 1982 in Cleveland, making him a member of the [[Kardiac Kids]], before being traded back to the Eagles, where he played two more years from 1983 to 1984. His tenure in Philadelphia included tackling a young [[Jeff Fisher]] (who later became the head coach of the [[Tennessee Titans]] and [[Los Angeles Rams|St. Louis Rams]]) when playing against the [[Chicago Bears]], causing Fisher to break his leg.{{cite magazine | first=Michael | last=Silver | title=Making A Statement | date=October 7, 1996 | url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1008844/index.htm | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121103120742/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1008844/index.htm | url-status=dead | archive-date=November 3, 2012 | magazine=Sports Illustrated | access-date=January 5, 2013}} The two would later be rival head coaches and friends in the [[AFC Central]] division, and Fisher has credited his injury at the hands of Cowher with having the [[unintended consequence]] of propelling him into coaching. Cowher primarily played [[special teams]] during his playing career; subsequently, he placed emphasis on special teams during his coaching career. Cowher credits being a "[[bubble player]]" during his playing career with influencing his coaching career, feeling that such players work the hardest for a roster spot (and sometimes still get cut, hence the term "bubble player"), and thus make better head coaches than those with successful playing careers.{{citation needed|date=February 2014}} ==Coaching career== ===Assistant jobs=== Cowher began his coaching career in 1985 at age 28 under [[Marty Schottenheimer]] with the [[Cleveland Browns]]. Cowher, who had played under Schottenheimer in Cleveland when Schottenheimer was the team's defensive coordinator, stated that he took a coaching position despite taking a significant pay cut from what he would have made as a player with the Eagles in 1985 because he saw his fortunes as a player limited and saw more of a future as a coach.{{Cite web | url=https://m.youtube.com/watch?feature=youtu.be&v=XKIKzV0Cy2w | title=- YouTube | website=[[YouTube]] | access-date=October 25, 2020 | archive-date=April 12, 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230412040540/https://m.youtube.com/watch?feature=youtu.be&v=XKIKzV0Cy2w | url-status=dead }} Cowher was the Browns' special teams coach in 1985–86 and secondary coach in 1987–88, during which he formed a bond with [[New York Giants]] [[defensive coordinator]] [[Bill Belichick]] and helped Belichick learn how to coach defensive backs while teaching Cowher how to coach linebackers. Belichick was impressed enough with Cowher that he and Giants head coach [[Bill Parcells]] offered to make Cowher the Giants defensive backs coach following Schottenheimer's sudden departure from Cleveland in 1988, but Cowher opted to remain loyal to Schottenheimer.{{cite web |url=https://steelersdepot.com/2023/10/bill-cowher-almost-became-the-cleveland-browns-head-coach-in-1991/ |title=Bill Cowher Almost Became the Cleveland Browns Head Coach in 1991 |website=SteelersDepot.com |last=Koroza |first=Adam |date=October 26, 2023 |access-date=January 23, 2025}} Following Schottenheimer to the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in 1989, Cowher was named defensive coordinator, becoming close with legendary Chiefs linebacker [[Derrick Thomas]].{{cite web |url=https://www.wtae.com/article/bill-cowher-tours-pro-football-hall-of-fame-ahead-of-his-induction/31106267 |title=Bill Cowher tours Pro Football Hall of Fame ahead of his induction |work=[[WTAE-TV|WTAE]] |date=February 25, 2020 |access-date=January 23, 2025}} He interviewed with the Browns for their head coaching vacancy in 1991 before losing out to close friend Belichick; it is believed that Cowher's young age at the time played a factor in losing out to Belichick. Cowher was a finalist for the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] head coaching position in 1991 following the dismissal of [[Sam Wyche]], but was passed over in favor of [[Dave Shula]]. ===Pittsburgh Steelers=== [[File:Bill Cowher September 1996.jpg|thumb|Cowher in 1996]] Cowher became the 15th head coach in Steelers history when he succeeded [[Chuck Noll]] on January 21, 1992 – but only the team's second head coach since the NFL merger in 1970, beating out fellow Pittsburgh native and [[Pittsburgh Panthers football|Pitt]] alumnus (and eventual Pitt head coach) [[Dave Wannstedt]] (Wannstedt instead became the coach of the Chicago Bears the following season).{{cite magazine | url=https://www.si.com/vault/1992/01/13/125777/thanks-but-no-thanks-as-others-scrambled-for-coaching-jobs-bill-parcells-rejected-two-whopping-offers# | title=Thanks, But No Thanks: As others scrambled for coaching jobs, Bill Parcells rejected two whopping offers | first=Peter | last=King | date=January 13, 1992 | magazine=Sports Illustrated | access-date=January 6, 2019}} Cowher continued a trend for the Steelers hiring coaches in their 30s that dates back to [[Joe Bach]] who began coaching the Steelers in 1935 when they were still named the Pittsburgh Pirates. Under Cowher, the Steelers showed an immediate improvement from the disappointing 7–9 season the year before, going 11–5 and earning home-field advantage in the AFC after the Steelers had missed the playoffs six times out of the previous seven years. His first season as a head coach came to an end in the AFC Divisional round on January 9, 1993, against the [[Buffalo Bills]] in which the Steelers would lose 24–3.{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199301090pit.htm|title=Divisional Round - Buffalo Bills at Pittsburgh Steelers - January 9th, 1993|website=[[Pro Football Reference]]}} [[Image:Bill Cowher challenge.jpg|250x250px|left|thumb|Cowher challenges a play]] The following season ended with a record of 9–7 for the Steelers. Under Cowher, the team scored a total of 308 points and allowed just 281 points against them.{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/pit/1993.htm|title=1993 Pittsburgh Steelers Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees|website=[[Pro Football Reference]]}} Though the Steelers fell 27–24 in the Wild Card Round to the [[Kansas City Chiefs]], it became the first time in a decade the Steelers had back-to-back playoff appearances.{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/pit/playoffs.htm|title=Pittsburgh Steelers Playoff History|website=[[Pro Football Reference]]}} In the 1995 regular season, Cowher got the team to record 11 wins and five losses, once again sending them to the playoffs and earned them a first round bye.{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/pit/1995.htm|title=1995 Pittsburgh Steelers Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees|website=[[Pro Football Reference]]}} The Steelers were able to defeat the [[Buffalo Bills]], who were coming off of four straight Super Bowl appearances, 40–24 and recorded a 20–16 victory against the [[Indianapolis Colts]]. Their win against the Colts made the Steelers AFC Champions for the first time since the [[1979 Pittsburgh Steelers season|1979 season]]. At age 38, he became the youngest coach to lead his team to a [[Super Bowl]], which the Steelers lost 27–17 to the [[Dallas Cowboys]]. Cowher is only the second coach in NFL history to lead his team to the playoffs in each of his first six seasons as head coach, joining [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] member Paul Brown. In [[1998 Pittsburgh Steelers season|1998]], Cowher led the team to their first losing season of his tenure, breaking a six-year streak of playoff teams. With quarterback [[Kordell Stewart]] at the helm, Cowher and the team finished with a record of 7-9 and placing third in the [[AFC Central]].{{cite web | title=1998 Pittsburgh Steelers Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees | website=[[Pro Football Reference]] | date=September 6, 1998 | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/pit/1998.htm | access-date=November 20, 2024}} [[1999 Pittsburgh Steelers season|The following season]], Pittsburgh would see a second consecutive losing season for the first time since [[List of Pittsburgh Steelers seasons|the 1985 and 1986 seasons]]. Despite a 4–3 start to the season heading into the [[bye (sports)|bye week]], the Steelers would go 2–7 on the remainder of the season to finish with a record of 6–10.{{cite web | title=1999 Pittsburgh Steelers Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees | website=[[Pro Football Reference]] | date=September 12, 1999 | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/pit/1999.htm | access-date=November 20, 2024}} [[File:Casey Hampton and Bill Cowher pregame 2006-11-26 (cropped).jpg|thumb|Cowher in 2006]] During the late 1990s and early 2000s, Cowher became known for drafting lineman with first round picks, which drew criticism from [[Steeler Nation|Steelers fans]]. During his tenure, the team had mixed results with this strategy, drafting future Hall of Famer [[Alan Faneca]] and future [[Pro Bowl]]ers [[Leon Searcy]] & [[Casey Hampton]] but also drafting [[Jamain Stephens]] (who would go on to be one of the team's biggest first-round busts) and [[Kendall Simmons]] (a solid starter but plagued by injuries and a sudden diagnosis of [[type 1 diabetes]]), with Stephens infamously being cut after failing the [[40-yard dash]] on the first day of training camp.{{cite web | title=A History of the Pittsburgh Steelers and the NFL Draft, Part 6: Offensive Linemen | website=Behind the Steel Curtain | date=April 22, 2022 | url=https://www.behindthesteelcurtain.com/2022/4/22/23027199/a-history-of-the-pittsburgh-steelers-and-the-nfl-draft-part-6-offensive-linemen-decastro-pouncey | access-date=November 18, 2024}} Between 1992 and 2002, the Steelers drafted five linemen on both the defensive and offensive sides in the first round, making up nearly half of Cowher's [[List of Pittsburgh Steelers first-round draft picks|first round picks]] in the first decade of his tenure. Defendants of this strategy pointed out that of the five lineman drafted, only Stephens was a bonafide bust and of the skill position players the Steelers did draft with their first round picks ([[Deon Figures]], [[Charles Johnson (wide receiver, born 1972)|Charles Johnson]], [[Mark Bruener]], [[Chad Scott]], [[Troy Edwards]], and [[Plaxico Burress]]), with the exception of Bruener--who despite being a [[tight end]] was more of a blocking tight end and a [[de facto]] sixth offensive lineman when he played--and to a lesser extent Scott and Burress largely didn't live up to expectations, though only Edwards would be a bust. (Notably, the Steelers drafted Edwards and Burress, both [[wide receiver]]s, despite having third-round pick [[Hines Ward]] already on their roster to replace Johnson and [[Yancey Thigpen]] following their departures in free agency; Ward would outright supplant Edwards on the depth chart by 2000.) Cowher's draft picks began to focus on skill positions in 2003 when cornerstone defensive back [[Troy Polamalu]] was taken with the 16th overall pick. The 2003 season would prove challenging for Cowher and the Steelers when the team was only able to win six of their 16 regular season games, missing the playoffs. Due to their poor record, it allowed for Cowher's team to draft [[Ben Roethlisberger]] with the 11th overall pick in the [[2004 NFL draft]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/pit/2003.htm|title=2003 Pittsburgh Steelers Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees|website=[[Pro Football Reference]]}} Cowher did not initially want to select Roethlisberger in the first round as he was "comfortable" with starter [[Tommy Maddox]] and backup [[Charlie Batch]].{{cite web | title=Big Ben & Coach Cowher talk 2004 draft, SB XL, getting Jerome Bettis to return and more! Ep. 27 | website=YouTube | date=March 6, 2024 | url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pNOkc67Jqlg | access-date=November 18, 2024}} His original decision was to draft [[Shawn Andrews (American football)|Shawn Andrews]], an offensive tackle from the [[University of Arkansas]]. Before the pick could be sent in during the draft, Steelers owner [[Dan Rooney]] overrode the decision and took Roethlisberger.{{Cite web |last=Brown |first=Scott |date=April 24, 2014 |title=Big Ben pick returned Steelers to glory |url=https://www.espn.com/blog/pittsburgh-steelers/post/_/id/6043/big-ben-pick-returned-steelers-to-glory |access-date=May 2, 2022 |website=ESPN.com |language=en |archive-date=October 26, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211026184201/https://www.espn.com/blog/pittsburgh-steelers/post/_/id/6043/big-ben-pick-returned-steelers-to-glory |url-status=live}} Cowher and the team would rebound from their previous season with a record of 15–1, earning a first round bye in the playoffs yet again. The Steelers would make another AFC Championship appearance, losing 41–27 to eventual Super Bowl champions the [[New England Patriots]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/pit/2004.htm|title=2004 Pittsburgh Steelers Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees|website=[[Pro Football Reference]]}} [[File:Bill Cowher.jpg|thumb|left|Cowher with the Steelers at the [[White House]] following their Super Bowl XL victory]] In 2005, the Steelers were able to clinch a spot in the playoffs with an 11–5 record as the #6-seed in the AFC.{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2005/playoffs.htm|title=2005 NFL Playoff Standings|website=[[Pro Football Reference]]}} The Steelers led an upset playoff run, including a 21–18 victory over the [[Indianapolis Colts]], the top seeded team in the AFC.{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/clt/2005.htm|title=2005 Indianapolis Colts Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees|website=[[Pro Football Reference]]}} Cowher would win his second AFC Championship on January 22, 2006, when the Steelers defeated the [[Denver Broncos]] 34–17.{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200601220den.htm|title=AFC Championship - Pittsburgh Steelers at Denver Broncos - January 22nd, 2006|website=[[Pro Football Reference]]}} On February 5, 2006, Cowher's Pittsburgh Steelers won [[Super Bowl XL]] by defeating the [[Seattle Seahawks]] 21–10, giving Cowher his first [[Super Bowl ring]] and making the Steelers the first sixth seed to win a Super Bowl in NFL history. Including the Super Bowl, Cowher's teams over the years had compiled a record of 108–1–1 in games in which they built a lead of at least 11 points.{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=brINAAAAIBAJ&dq=ike-taylor&pg=4176%2C4057270|title=Taylor's interception clips Seahawk's wings|last=Collier|first=Gene|date=February 6, 2006|newspaper=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]|access-date=March 29, 2010}}{{Dead link|date=August 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} On January 5, 2007, Cowher resigned after 15 years of being the Steelers head coach. Cowher's record as a head coach was 161–99–1, including the playoffs. He was succeeded by [[Mike Tomlin]]. In Cowher's 15 seasons, the Steelers captured eight division titles, earned 10 postseason playoff berths (including six straight in his first six seasons), played in 21 playoff games, advanced to six [[American Football Conference|AFC]] Championship games and made two Super Bowl appearances. He is one of only six coaches in NFL history to claim at least seven division titles. At the conclusion of the 2005 season, the Steelers had the best record of any team in the NFL since Cowher was hired as head coach. On January 11, 2020, Cowher was told live on a CBS pregame show that he was being inducted into the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] as part of its centennial class by its president [[C. David Baker|David Baker]].''The NFL Today''. CBS. January 11, 2020. ====Coaching philosophy and legacy==== Much like his mentor Marty Schottenheimer, Cowher believed in a strong defense with an emphasis on special teams performance, complimented by a strong running game on offense. Unlike the conservative Schottenheimer, however, Cowher was known to take more risks, including going for it on fourth down, such as his first game as a head coach against the [[Houston Oilers]] when he had punter [[Mark Royals]] throw a fake punt to [[Warren Williams (American football)|Warren Williams]], putting the Steelers near the goal line.{{Cite web |date=November 27, 2020 |title=Exclusive with Former Steelers Punter Mark Royals, 1992-1994 – Welcome to Steelers Takeaways! |url=https://steelerstakeaways.com/exclusive-with-former-steelers-punter-mark-royals-1992-1994/ |access-date=November 8, 2024 |language=en-US}} Unlike the stoic Noll, Cowher was known to be more fiery and emotional, specifically with his jaw line when he was angry and being known as "the Chin".{{Cite web |last=DiPerna |first=Jody |year=2006 |title=Bill Cowher Keeps His Chin Up |url=https://www.pghcitypaper.com/columns/bill-cowher-keeps-his-chin-up-1334120 |access-date=November 8, 2024 |website=Pittsburgh City Paper |language=en}} This was exemplified in a 1995 game against the [[Minnesota Vikings]] when the referees mistakenly [[Penalty (gridiron football)|penalized]] the Steelers for 12 men on the field following a missed field goal. The Vikings made the subsequent rekick despite Cowher's protests that they had the regulated 11 players on the field, and stuffed an "all-22" photo as proof into referee [[Gordon McCarter]]'s pocket, leading to a $7,500 fine by the NFL for Cowher putting his hands on an official.{{Cite web |last=Carney |first=Josh |date=May 9, 2023 |title='A Great Teaching Moment For Me': Bill Cowher Recalls Infamous Polaroid Incident With Official |url=https://steelersdepot.com/2023/05/a-great-teaching-moment-for-me-bill-cowher-recalls-infamous-polaroid-incident-with-official/ |access-date=November 8, 2024 |website=Steelers Depot |language=en-US}} Cowher is also known for being a vocal supporter of the coaching profession in general and was upset that the [[Indianapolis Colts]] hired former center [[Jeff Saturday]] as interim head coach in 2022 despite having no coaching experience above the [[High school football|high school]] level and the team having several assistants already on the staff with previous head coaching experience.{{Cite web |last=Lemoncelli |first=Jenna |date=November 16, 2022 |title=Pat McAfee calls out Bill Cowher over Colts, Jeff Saturday remarks |url=https://nypost.com/2022/11/16/pat-mcafee-calls-out-bill-cowher-over-colts-jeff-saturday-remarks/ |access-date=July 28, 2023 |website=NYPost.com |language=en-US}} ==After coaching== [[File:Dan Marino, Bill Cowher en el CBS Pre-game Show (4406601512).jpg|250x250px|thumb|[[Dan Marino]] and Cowher during a CBS Pre-game Show in 2010]] On February 15, 2007, Cowher signed on to ''[[The NFL Today]]'' on [[CBS]] as a studio analyst, joining [[Dan Marino]], [[Shannon Sharpe]], and [[Boomer Esiason]]. Cowher also serves as a host of the NFL's CBS Halftime Report. In November 2024, he confirmed that he would re-sign with CBS in 2025, keeping him as a host for 19 years.{{cite web | last=Marczi | first=Matthew | title=Bill Cowher Confirms He Will Remain On 'The NFL Today' Show Through 2025 | website=Steelers Depot | date=November 18, 2024| url=https://steelersdepot.com/2024/11/bill-cowher-confirms-he-will-remain-on-the-nfl-today-show-through-2025/ | access-date=November 19, 2024}} In 2007, Cowher appeared in the [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]] reality television series ''[[Fast Cars and Superstars: The Gillette Young Guns Celebrity Race]]'', featuring a dozen celebrities in a stock car racing competition. He matched up against [[Gabrielle Reece]] and [[William Shatner]]. On March 4, 2008, Cowher responded to rumors concerning his coaching future by stating, "I'm not going anywhere."{{cite news | first=Ed | last=Bouchette | title=Cowhers will move, but not to Penn State | date=March 5, 2008 | url =http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/08065/862482-66.stm | work=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette | access-date = March 7, 2008 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080308181250/http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/08065/862482-66.stm| archive-date= March 8, 2008 | url-status= live}} The rumors started after the Cowhers placed their [[Raleigh, North Carolina|Raleigh]], North Carolina home on the market, but their intention was to build a new house two miles away. Putting an end to numerous unfounded rumors of his return to coaching in the NFL in 2009, Cowher stated on ''[[The NFL Today]]'' that he did not plan to coach again in the immediate future.{{cite news|url=https://www.tsn.ca/nfl/story/?id=261929&lid=sublink05&lpos=headlines_main|title=Cowher Doesn't Plan on Coaching in 2009|date=January 4, 2009|publisher=TSN|access-date=January 4, 2009}} In July 2010, Cowher was the keynote speaker for National Agents Alliance at their Leadership Conference. He talked about work ethic, [[leadership]] and how that transfers into the work force. Cowher said that it is not about what you accomplish, it is about who you touch along the way.{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TlfVx7A1i3w | archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211104/TlfVx7A1i3w| archive-date=November 4, 2021 | url-status=live| title=Bill Cowher talks to National Agents Alliance Agents about opportunity and hard work| website=[[YouTube]]| date=August 23, 2010}}{{cbignore}} Cowher had a part in the movie ''[[The Dark Knight Rises]]'' (2012), which was filmed at [[Heinz Field]], the home of the Steelers, on Pittsburgh's North Side. He played the head coach of the Gotham Rogues.{{cite web |author=Aaron on |url=http://my.spill.com/profiles/blog/show?id=947994:BlogPost:3851482 |title=Aaron's Experience As An Extra On 'The Dark '''Bertrand Demond Berry''' (born August 15, 1975) is an American former professional [[Gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame Fighting Irish]].

==Early life==
Berry, whose nickname is "King" started his football career in the Humble Area Football League with the Cardinals as a running back.[http://www.humblefootball.org HAFL]
Berry attended [[Humble High School]] in [[Humble, Texas]], and was a star running back for the Wildcats.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=BERRYBER01 |title=Bert Berry |publisher=databaseFootball.com |accessdate=October 19, 2012 |url-status=usurped |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20121017113530/http://databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=BerryBer01 |archivedate=October 17, 2012 }}</ref> where he was a three-sport standout in [[basketball]], [[High school football|football]], and [[Track and field|track]]. In basketball, he was a two-time all-district selection, and in track, he threw the [[discus]] and set the school record for the shuttle hurdle relays.

==College career==
Berry attended the [[University of Notre Dame]] and was a four-year [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] in [[College football|football]]. He finished his [[NCAA]] football career with 187 tackles and 16.5 sacks.

==Professional career==
Berry was selected by the [[Indianapolis Colts]] in the third round of the [[1997 NFL draft]], starting out as a [[linebacker]] before switching to defensive end.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1997 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1997/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-30 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He spent most of his time there playing between [[Defense (sport)|defense]] and [[special teams]], [[Starting lineup|starting]] most of the games on defense. He signed with the [[St. Louis Rams]] in [[2000 NFL season|2000]], but was cut during training camp.

He signed with the [[Edmonton Eskimos]] of the [[Canadian Football League]] on September 26, 2000, on October 11 after seeing action in two games. He recorded one tackle in his two appearances.

By the [[2003 NFL season|2003 season]] with the [[Denver Broncos]], he was the starter at defensive end and led the team in tackles and sacks. He was picked up as a [[free agent]] by Arizona before the [[2004 NFL season|2004 season]], during which he was named as a starter to represent the [[National Football Conference|NFC]] in the [[2005 Pro Bowl]].

On March 18, 2009, Berry agreed to a one-year contract.

On January 21, 2010, Berry announced his retirement from the NFL. He finished his career with 232 total tackles, 65 sacks and 13 forced fumbles.

==Broadcasting career==
In August 2011, Berry began hosting a radio show on The Fan AM 1060 [[KDUS]] in [[Phoenix, Arizona|Phoenix]] called ''The Bertrand Berry Show'' with Mike Grose every weekday from 1:00 to 3:00. The show was cancelled effective December 28, 2012.

On April 23, 2015, Berry had a fill-in role for Ron Wolfley on the ''Doug and Wolf Show'' on Arizona Sports 98.7 FM, a local Arizona radio station. On August 3, Berry began hosting "Off the Edge with B-Train" on [[KMVP-FM|Arizona Sports 98.7 FM]].

'''Bethel Johnson '''(born February 11, 1979) is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[New England Patriots]] in the second round of the [[2003 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] for [[Texas A&M Aggies football|Texas A&M Aggies]].

Johnson earned two [[Super Bowl ring]]s with the Patriots in [[Super Bowl XXXVIII]] and [[Super Bowl XXXIX]]. He was also a member of the [[New Orleans Saints]], [[Minnesota Vikings]], [[Philadelphia Eagles]], [[Houston Texans]] and [[Toronto Argonauts]].

==Early life==
Johnson attended [[Corsicana High School]] in [[Corsicana, Texas]] and as a senior, he led his team to the Class 4A state title game, and made 44 receptions for 1495 yards and 17 receiving touchdowns.

==College career==
Johnson attended [[Texas A&M University]], and finished his [[college football]] career with 117 receptions for 1740 yards (14.9 yards per reception), and 11 receiving touchdowns. His 117 receptions and 1740 receiving yards both rank second in school career records.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aggieathletics.com/records.php?SID=MFB&funct=21&type=2&list=16 |title=Most Receiving Yards - Career |publisher=Texas A&M Athletics |access-date=May 26, 2008 |archive-date=December 15, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191215203354/http://www.aggieathletics.com/records.php?SID=MFB&funct=21&type=2&list=16 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aggieathletics.com/records.php?SID=MFB&funct=20&type=2&list=17 |title=Most Receptions - Career |publisher=Texas A&M Athletics |access-date=May 26, 2008 |archive-date=December 15, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191215203351/http://www.aggieathletics.com/records.php?SID=MFB&funct=20&type=2&list=17 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

*Sophomore - 27 catches for 514 yards and 3 TD.
*Junior - 42 catches for 440 yards and 0 TD.
*Redshirt Senior - 40 catches for 718 yards and 8 TD.  He also averaged 21 yards per KR and 11.6 yards per PR.

===New England Patriots===
Johnson was selected 45th overall in the [[2003 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2003 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2003/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-28 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>  In his rookie season, ranked second in the NFL with a 28.2 yards per kickoff return average, returning 30 kickoffs for 847 yards and a touchdown, while also catching 16 passes for 209 yards and 2 scores. In [[Super Bowl XXXVIII|2003]] and [[Super Bowl XXXIX|2004]] he won the [[Super Bowl]] with the [[New England Patriots]].

===New Orleans Saints===
He was traded to the Saints on June 5, 2006, for [[defensive tackle]] [[Johnathan Sullivan (American football)|Johnathan Sullivan]], who was drafted sixth overall by the Saints in [[2003 NFL draft|2003]]. Saints coach, [[Sean Payton]], questioned Johnson's "conditioning, his stamina and endurance" during the preseason.<ref>[http://www.twincities.com/mld/twincities/sports/football/15783737.htm HOME - TwinCities.com<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>

Johnson was cut from the Saints before the [[2006 NFL season|2006]] regular season began after injuring his knee in a preseason game.

===Minnesota Vikings===
Johnson was then signed by the [[Minnesota Vikings]] on October 10, 2006.<ref>{{cite news| url=http://www.boston.com/sports/football/patriots/articles/2006/09/05/hes_ready_for_some_football/?page=2 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070311092335/http://www.boston.com/sports/football/patriots/articles/2006/09/05/hes_ready_for_some_football/?page=2 | url-status=dead | archive-date=March 11, 2007 | work=The Boston Globe | title=He's ready for some football | date=September 5, 2006 | first=Mike | last=Reiss}}</ref> He appeared in 11 games with two starts for the Vikings that season, catching nine passes for 156 yards. He became a [[free agent]] in the [[2007 NFL season|2007 offseason]].

===Philadelphia Eagles===
On March 8, 2007, he signed a one-year contract with the Philadelphia Eagles. He was released on June 5, after he failed a physical.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://nfl.com/nflnetwork/story/10214359|title=Samuel holding out for a new deal with Pats|last=Schefter|first=Adam |date=June 5, 2007|work=NFL.com|access-date=June 7, 2008| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070707051313/http://nfl.com/nflnetwork/story/10214359| archive-date=July 7, 2007|quote=The Eagles cut wide receiver/kick returner Bethel Johnson after he failed his physical.}}</ref>

===Houston Texans===
On July 9, 2007, Johnson signed with the [[Houston Texans]]. However, he was released on August 31, during final cuts and spent the rest of the season out of football.

===Toronto Argonauts===
On May 26, 2008, Johnson was signed by the [[Toronto Argonauts]] of the [[Canadian Football League]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cbc.ca/sports/football/argonauts-add-former-nfler-bethel-johnson-1.720244|title=Argonauts add former NFLer Bethel Johnson|date=May 26, 2008|publisher=CBC Sports|access-date=October 1, 2008}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.thestar.com/article/447495|title=Johnson looking to start over with Argos|last=Zelkovich|first=Chris|date=June 23, 2008|publisher=Toronto Star|access-date=June 23, 2008}}</ref> He was released on September 30, due to his lack of progress; ranking just seventh on the team in receiving with 16 catches for 189 yards and no touchdowns.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://nationalpost.com/sports/story.html?id=851288 |title=Johnson cut as Argos continue reworking roster |last=Fitz-Gerald |first=Sean |date=September 30, 2008 |publisher=National Post |access-date=October 1, 2008 }}{{dead link|date=October 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>
