'''Bernard Joseph Kosar Jr.''' (born November 25, 1963) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Miami Hurricanes football|Miami Hurricanes]], leading the team to a [[1983 NCAA Division I-A football rankings|national championship in 1983]]. He subsequently played in the NFL for the [[Cleveland Browns]] from 1985 to 1993, the [[Dallas Cowboys]] in 1993, and [[Miami Dolphins]] from 1994 to 1996. He was the backup quarterback on the [[1993 Dallas Cowboys season|1993 Cowboys team]] that won [[Super Bowl XXVIII]].

==Early life==
Kosar was born in [[Youngstown, Ohio]] and raised in suburban [[Boardman Township, Mahoning County, Ohio|Boardman Township]]. He is of [[Hungarian Americans|Hungarian descent]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Balogh |first=András |date=2021-02-06 |title=Hungarians in the history of the NFL |url=https://dailynewshungary.com/hungarians-in-the-history-of-nfl/ |access-date=2026-01-13 |language=en-US}}</ref>

He attended [[Boardman High School]], where he earned ''[[Parade (magazine)|Parade]]'' magazine [[All-American]] honors in 1981 as a senior and was [[Ohio]]'s Division I "Player of the Year." He also gained recognition as a baseball player, especially for his [[pitcher|pitching]] skills.<ref name="brownsnation.com">[https://www.brownsnation.com/bernie-kosar/ "The legend of Browns QB Bernie Kosar (Complete Story)"], by Ben Donahue, Browns Nation, May 20, 2020, retrieved February 20, 2022.</ref>

==College career==
[[File:President Ronald Reagan Throwing a Football During a Photo Op with Football Player Bernie Kosar of The Cleveland Browns with An Unidentified Women in The Oval Office - DPLA - 5187a9336c4f27149c9caab464567290.jpg|thumb|Kosar with U.S. President [[Ronald Reagan]] in the [[Oval Office]] in February 1987]]
Kosar was recruited by [[University of Miami]] head football coach [[Howard Schnellenberger]], and Kosar committed to the [[Miami Hurricanes football|University of Miami]], which ran a passing-oriented offense and was beginning to emerge as one of the nation's premier [[college football]] programs. Kosar proved instrumental in establishing the University of Miami nickname "[[Quarterback U]]" in reference to the number of top quarterbacks the program produced.<ref name="HOF">[https://www.umsportshalloffame.com/bernie-kosar.html Bernie Kosar at University of Miami Hall of Fame], retrieved February 20, 2022.</ref>

After being [[redshirt (college sports)|redshirted]] in 1982, Kosar [[Starting lineup|started]] all 12 games as a freshman in 1983. In the 1983 season, he completed 61.5 percent of his passes for 2,328 yards and 15 touchdowns, leading the Hurricanes to an 11–1 regular season and a berth in the [[Orange Bowl]] against top-ranked [[Nebraska Cornhuskers football|Nebraska]], which had won 22 consecutive games. In the game, Kosar passed for 300 yards and two touchdowns, and the Hurricanes topped the Cornhuskers, 31–30, for [[1983 Miami Hurricanes football team|Miami's first national championship]]. Kosar earned Orange Bowl MVP honors for his performance.<ref>Cleveland Browns 1992 Media Guide</ref>

In 1984, he set Hurricane season records with 3,642 yards and 25 touchdowns, was a second-team All-American and finished fourth in [[Heisman Trophy]] voting. Kosar's career completion percentage of 62.3 percent is still a Hurricanes record.<ref name="HOF" />

Kosar threw for 447 yards and two touchdowns, completing 25 of 38 attempts, in the Hurricanes' November 23, 1984, 47–45 loss to [[Boston College]] when Flutie threw his famous "[[Hail Flutie]]" pass.<ref>ESPN College Football Encyclopedia, ESPN Books, (2005), {{ISBN|1-4013-3703-1}}.  p. 160</ref>  Earlier the same year, Kosar watched as replacement quarterback [[Frank Reich]] of the [[Maryland Terrapins football|Maryland Terrapins]] launched what was then the biggest comeback in college football history, coming back from a first-half deficit of 31–0 to win a 42–40 victory.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.umterps.com/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_LANG=C&DB_OEM_ID=29700&ATCLID=208126792&SPID=120713&SPSID=716333|title=Maryland Football Quarterback Legacy|publisher=University of Maryland|access-date=December 29, 2017}}</ref> The game and pass have been described as among the most memorable moments in sports history.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://msn.foxsports.com/nfl/story/Ten-Best-Damn-unforgettable-sports-moments|title=Ten Best Damn unforgettable sports moments – NFL News | FOX Sports on MSN|date=May 16, 2014|access-date=February 21, 2022|archive-date=May 16, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140516222405/http://msn.foxsports.com/nfl/story/Ten-Best-Damn-unforgettable-sports-moments|url-status=bot: unknown}}</ref>

His final collegiate game was the 1985 [[Fiesta Bowl]] against [[University of California, Los Angeles|UCLA]], which the Hurricanes lost 39–37. In that game, Kosar completed 31 of 44 passes for 294 yards, two touchdown passes and one interception.

Kosar graduated from the [[Miami Herbert Business School|University of Miami School of Business]] with a double major in finance and economics. He took 18 credit hours during the spring of 1985 and an additional six during the summer to graduate early.<ref>1992 cleveland browns media guide</ref>

Kosar was interviewed about his time at the University of Miami for the documentary ''[[The U (film)|The U]]'', which premiered on [[ESPN]] on December 12, 2009.

==Professional career==
===NFL draft controversy===
[[File:Bernie Kosar 1985.jpg|thumb|Kosar in 1985]]
In 1985, Kosar was a highly sought NFL prospect, described as having "an elite football IQ" and "being able to decipher a defense quicker than his coaches."<ref name="brownsnation.com"/> But his route from the [[University of Miami]] to the [[National Football League]] would prove to be filled with widespread controversy and the use of highly unconventional transactional and draft NFL tactics.<ref name="news5cleveland.com">[https://www.news5cleveland.com/sports/2021-nfl-draft/the-remarkable-tale-of-how-bernie-kosar-bypassed-the-regular-nfl-draft-to-join-the-cleveland-browns "How Bernie Kosar bypassed the regular NFL draft to join the Cleveland Browns," News 5 Cleveland, April 29, 2021], retrieved February 20, 2022</ref>

In a March 14, 1985 press conference in [[Miami]], Kosar announced that he was forgoing his final two years of collegiate eligibility at the University of Miami to enter the National Football League. Kosar grew up a [[Cleveland Browns]] fan,<ref name="Bernie Kosar">[https://www.brownsnation.com/bernie-kosar/ "Bernie Kosar"] at Browns Nation</ref> and also announced in the press conference that he would like to play for the Browns in his native Ohio.

NFL rules at the time permitted only college seniors and college graduates to enter the [[1985 NFL draft]], and Kosar was still a University of Miami underclassman in March 1985. To establish eligibility, Kosar announced he had arranged an expedited academic plan with 18 credits in spring 1985 and an additional six credits in the summer that would permit him to graduate from the University of Miami in time to meet the draft's eligibility requirements. In June 1985, the University of Miami notified the NFL that Kosar had met the course requirements to graduate.<ref name="Bernie Kosar"/>

Seeking to obtain Kosar in the NFL draft, the [[Minnesota Vikings]] on April 9, 1985, traded with the [[History of the Houston Oilers|Houston Oilers]] to obtain a top draft selection and announced their intent to draft Kosar. Meanwhile, also seeking to draft Kosar, the Browns quietly traded their first round NFL draft selections for 1985 and 1986, their third round selection in 1985 and sixth selection in 1986 with the [[Buffalo Bills]] for the Bills' first pick in the 1985 supplemental draft, which paved the way for the Browns to select Kosar in the 1985 supplemental draft if Kosar entered it.<ref name="news5cleveland.com"/>

The NFL deadline for the submission of formal eligibility documents for the 1985 draft was April 15, 1985, and the Vikings learned that Kosar had not met the deadline. "I'm as confused as you are," Vikings coach [[Bud Grant]] said at the time about Kosar. "We put our bid on the line. It's up to the commissioner whether you need a verbal or a written commitment from the man. He dropped out of football, hired an agent and declared he was going in the draft. The only thing he didn't do was sign a letter."<ref>[https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1985-04-23-8501240241-story.html "Grant's foes like Kosar's direction,"] ''Chicago Tribune'', April 23, 1985, retrieved February 22, 2022.</ref>

Teams soon learned of the Browns' highly unorthodox trade with the Bills to obtain Kosar in the supplemental draft. Several teams asked then NFL Commissioner [[Pete Rozelle]] to prevent the unusual trade between the Browns and Bills. Rozelle, in turn, announced that he was giving Kosar until April 23 to submit eligibility documents for either the traditional or supplemental draft. On April 25, Kosar held a press conference, announcing his intention to skip the traditional draft and enter the supplemental draft, where he expected to be selected with the Browns' first selection.<ref name="Bernie Kosar"/>

The [[Houston Texans|Houston Oilers]], also seeking to draft Kosar in the traditional draft, threatened to sue to stop the entire draft unless Kosar was in it. Houston also appealed to the Vikings to join the suit. Kosar's agent, in turn, threatened to sue the NFL if Kosar was obligated to enter the traditional draft.

But when the Vikings refused to join the suit, the Oilers dropped it. Kosar submitted documentation announcing his eligibility and participation in the 1985 supplemental draft.<ref name="news5cleveland.com"/>

On July 3, 1985, the Browns used their first selection in the 1985 supplemental draft to select Kosar, offering him a five-year contract.<ref name="Bernie Kosar"/><ref>{{Cite web |title=1985 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1985/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-05 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

===Cleveland Browns===
The [[Cleveland Browns]] intended for Kosar to serve as [[Gary Danielson]]'s backup in Kosar's rookie season, but Danielson injured his shoulder in the fifth week. Kosar completed half of his passes in the team's run-oriented offense that year, and the team squeaked into the playoffs with an 8–8 record, losing to the [[Miami Dolphins]] in the divisional playoffs.

Danielson was injured again in the 1986 preseason. By the time Danielson healed and returned, however, Kosar had established himself as the Browns' permanent starter. In a new, passing-focused offense, Kosar threw for 3,854 yards and finished second in the league with 310 completions. The Browns took the top seed in the [[American Football Conference]] (AFC) with a 12–4 record.  In the divisional playoffs against the [[New York Jets]], Kosar threw for a then-playoff-record 489 yards (a record since broken by [[Tom Brady]] in [[Super Bowl LII]]) in leading the Browns to a 23–20 comeback victory in double overtime. But the following week, [[John Elway]]'s [[The Drive (American football)|98-yard drive]] in the [[1986–87 NFL playoffs#AFC Championship: Denver Broncos 23, Cleveland Browns 20 (OT)|AFC championship game]] kept the Browns out of the [[Super Bowl]].

Kosar's most productive year statistically was 1987. In the strike-shortened season, he completed 62 percent of his passes for 3,033 yards and 22 touchdowns and led the AFC in quarterback rating. In an [[1987–88 NFL playoffs#AFC Championship: Denver Broncos 38, Cleveland Browns 33|AFC championship rematch]] against Elway's [[Denver Broncos]], Kosar threw for 356 yards and three touchdowns in a 38–33 loss, the game is remembered for a [[The Fumble|last minute fumble]] by Browns running back, [[Earnest Byner]]. 
[[File:Bernie Kosar with the Cleveland Browns (cropped).jpg|thumb|right|175px|Kosar with the Browns in 1988]]
Kosar spent most of the 1988 season sidelined with injuries but came back to throw for 3,533 yards in 1989.  That year, the Browns advanced to the AFC championship for the third time in four years, [[1989–90 NFL playoffs#AFC Championship: Denver Broncos 37, Cleveland Browns 21|losing again to the Broncos]] in Denver.

Kosar set a record for [[Most consecutive games with a touchdown pass (NFL)#All-time consecutive playoff games with at least three touchdown passes|consecutive playoff games with at least three touchdown passes (3 games)]] having thrown three scores against both [[Indianapolis Colts|Indianapolis]] and Denver in 1987, and three against [[Buffalo Bills|Buffalo]] in 1989.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/K/KosaBe00/gamelog|title=Bernie Kosar Career Game Log|publisher=Pro-football-reference.com|access-date=October 1, 2012}}</ref>

Kosar's later years in Cleveland were dampened by injuries and dwindling support around him. In 1990, Kosar threw a career-high 15 interceptions as the Browns went 3–13. He also started the 1990 season by setting an NFL record for consecutive pass attempts without an interception with 286.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://myespn.go.com/blogs/nfceast/0-5-23/Kosar-s-record-safe-from-Campbell.html | title=Kosar's Record Safe From Campbell | first=Matt | last=Mosley | date=November 3, 2008 | work=ESPN.com | access-date=October 26, 2018 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090123134720/http://myespn.go.com/blogs/nfceast/0-5-23/Kosar-s-record-safe-from-Campbell.html | archive-date=January 23, 2009}}</ref> The following year, 1991, Kosar came back to throw for 3,487 yards and 18 touchdowns to only 9 interceptions. In 1990 and 1991, Kosar set league records by throwing 308 consecutive passes without an interception, which stood as an AFC League record for almost two decades.

In 1991, the Browns hired [[Bill Belichick]] as head coach. Following a 1992 season that saw Kosar miss nine games with a broken ankle and go 2–5 in the games that he started, Belichick signed quarterback [[Vinny Testaverde]], also a former [[University of Miami]] quarterback, prior to the 1993 season. After falling from 3–0 to 3–2 in the 1993 season, Belichick benched Kosar in favor of Testaverde. An injury to Testaverde returned Kosar to the field. After a 29–14 loss to Denver in Week 10, the Browns released Kosar despite controversy and 
fan backlash.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1993/11/08/Browns-release-Kosar/5683752734800/|title=Browns release Kosar – UPI Archives|website=UPI}}</ref>

According to a poll of Browns fans in 2019, Kosar was considered the "most beloved" Browns player in the franchise's history.<ref>[https://www.brownsnation.com/most-beloved-cleveland-browns/ "Most beloved Cleveland Browns,"] Browns Nation, October 18, 2019], retrieved February 20, 2021.</ref>

===Dallas Cowboys===
The [[Dallas Cowboys]] suffered an injury to starter [[Troy Aikman]] on the same weekend.  After Kosar's release, the Cowboys promptly signed Kosar to a one-year, $1 million contract as the backup quarterback for rookie [[Jason Garrett]].  After an inefficient first nine minutes of the game against [[1993 Phoenix Cardinals season|Phoenix]] with only two completions, Garrett was replaced by Kosar, who finished the rest of the game and started the next game for his only two meaningful game action in the regular season.  During the [[1993–94 NFL playoffs#NFC Championship: Dallas Cowboys 38, San Francisco 49ers 21|NFC Championship Game]] against the [[1993 San Francisco 49ers season|San Francisco 49ers]], Aikman was knocked out of the game with a concussion in the third quarter, with Kosar finishing the game, completing five of nine pass attempts for 83 yards and one touchdown.  He earned his only [[Super Bowl]] championship as a backup in [[Super Bowl XXVIII]], entering the game in the final play and knelt down to close the victory.

===Miami Dolphins===
Kosar spent the final two years of his NFL career with the [[Miami Dolphins]] as backup to [[Dan Marino]]. Kosar brought to the Dolphins a trick play that helped the Dolphins top the [[New York Jets]] in a crucial 1994 game.<ref name="FakeSpike">{{cite web | url=http://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/11925261/the-fake-spike-20th-anniversary-miami-dolphins-unforgettable-victory-new-york-jets | title=The Fake Spike, 20 years later | first=Rich | last=Cimini | date=November 26, 2014 | website=ESPN.com | access-date=October 26, 2018}}</ref> With the clock winding down and the Dolphins trailing by three, Marino [[The Clock Play|pretended to spike the ball]] to stop the clock. He then threw the winning touchdown pass to [[Mark Ingram Sr.|Mark Ingram]].<ref name="FakeSpike" />

Kosar finished his 12-season career with 1,994 completions in 3,365 attempts for 23,301 yards and 124 touchdowns, 87 interceptions, and five rushing touchdowns.<ref>[https://www.nfl.com/players/bernie-kosar/stats/career "Bernie Kosar career statistics], NFL.com, retrieved February 22, 2022.</ref> In November 1991, Kosar also set the NFL record for most consecutive completed passes without an interception, a record that stood until broken by [[Tom Brady]] on December 26, 2010.<ref>[https://www.deseret.com/1991/11/11/18951141/kosar-passes-starr-in-error-free-passing "Kosar passes Starr in error-free passing,"], ''Deseret News'', November 11, 1991.</ref>

==Post-retirement==

===Sports-related===
Since his NFL retirement in 1996, Kosar has been involved in several sports and business-related ventures. He hosted the Nestlé/Bernie Kosar Charity Classic at [[Tanglewood National Golf Club]] in [[Bainbridge Township, Ohio]] throughout the 1990s.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.bernie-kosar.com/berniespeaks.html | title=Instead of Art, will it be Bernie? | first=Bart | last=Hubbuch | date=March 26, 1996 | work=Akron Beacon Journal | via=Bernie-kosar.com | access-date=October 26, 2018}}</ref>

In 2001, Kosar purchased the [[Florida Panthers]], a [[National Hockey League]] team, along with pharmaceutical businessman [[Alan Cohen]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/203067-bernies-bankupt-a-symbol-of-a-nation-generation-and-region | title=Bernie's Bankrupt: A Symbol of a Nation, Generation and Region? | first=Christopher | last=Maher | date=June 20, 2009 | website=BleacherReport.com | access-date=October 26, 2018}}</ref>

In 2007, there was some speculation that Kosar might take the head coaching job at the [[University of Miami]], his alma mater and where he holds a seat on the university's [[Governing boards of colleges and universities in the United States|board of regents]]. Kosar acknowledged that he had considered taking the job before it was ultimately offered to [[Randy Shannon]].<ref>[http://www.allheadlinenews.com/articles/7005767950 Kosar considering Miami coaching job] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929111301/http://www.allheadlinenews.com/articles/7005767950|date=September 29, 2007}}, AllHeadlineNews.com. URL accessed December 6, 2006</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.espn.com/college-football/news/story?id=2688010 | title=Kosar interested in returning to alma mater | agency=[[Associated Press]] | date=December 6, 2006 | website=ESPN.com | access-date=October 26, 2018}}</ref>

Kosar also purchased a minority share in the [[Arena Football League]]'s [[Las Vegas Gladiators]] in 2007 and announced that the team would move to [[Cleveland]] and play under the name [[Cleveland Gladiators]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Jay|first=Robbie|url=http://diehardfansanonymous.blogspot.com/2007/10/arena-football-coming-to-cleveland.html|title=Arena Football Coming to Cleveland|publisher=Die Hard Fans Anonymous|date=October 11, 2007|access-date=October 1, 2012}}</ref> On October 16, 2007, Kosar was named team president and CEO of the franchise.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/arena/news?slug=txarenacleveland&prov=st&type=lgns |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120714000952/http://sports.yahoo.com/arena/news?slug=txarenacleveland&prov=st&type=lgns |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 14, 2012 |title=Las Vegas franchise relocates to Cleveland for 2008 AFL season |publisher=Yahoo! Sports |date=November 30, 2010 |access-date=October 1, 2012 }}</ref> The Gladiators finished the 2008 regular season 9–7, earning them a playoff berth.

On October 17, 2009, Kosar was hired as a consultant for the [[Cleveland Browns]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.cleveland.com/browns/2009/10/bernies_back_--_kosar_joins_br.html|title=Bernie's back – Kosar joins Browns as consultant to Randy Lerner: NFL Insider | first=Tony | last=Grossi | date=October 17, 2009 | work=The Plain Dealer | location=Cleveland, Ohio | access-date=December 30, 2021}}</ref>

In September 2022, Kosar launched "The Bernie Kosar Show" with local sports media company BIGPLAY. A sports podcast with [[Cleveland Browns]] [[cornerback]] [[Hanford Dixon]] interviewing athletes and discussing the [[Cleveland Browns]] past present, and future.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://kosar19.com/|title=Bernie Kosar's Official Website | Kosar 19|website=kosar19.com}}</ref> In 2023 Kosar was involved in a lawsuit related to BIGPLAY.<ref name=pd20241202>{{cite news|first=Sean|last=McDonnell|title=Browns legend Bernie Kosar embroiled in litigation involving two business deals gone bad|url=https://www.cleveland.com/news/2024/11/browns-legend-bernie-kosar-embroiled-in-litigation-involving-two-business-deals-gone-bad.html|url-access=subscription|work=[[The Plain Dealer]]|date=December 2, 2024|access-date=December 5, 2024}}</ref>

===Business and property ventures===
Following the 2008–2009 recession, Kosar and his businesses declared bankruptcy on June 19, 2009, later revealing $9.2 million in assets and $18.9 million in debt. Kosar's initial bankruptcy filing was a [[Chapter 11 bankruptcy|Chapter 11]] restructuring, but the U.S. Bankruptcy Court in [[Fort Lauderdale, Florida|Ft. Lauderdale]] on January 6, 2010, ordered the proceeding be changed to a [[Chapter 7 bankruptcy|Chapter 7]] liquidation.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.cleveland.com/browns/2010/01/bernie_kosars_assets_will_be_s.html | title=Bernie Kosar's assets will be sold off | work=The Plain Dealer | location=Cleveland, Ohio | date=January 9, 2010 | access-date=December 30, 2021 | last=Bathon | first=Michael}}</ref> Under the restructuring, Kosar's filings proposed protecting his NFL pension, though it was unclear {{when|date=May 2013}} if this will be permitted under a Chapter 7 proceeding.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ecf.flsb.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/login.pl|title=ernard J. Kosar Jr., no. 09-22371, Bankr. S.D. Fla.|website=[[PACER (law)|PACER]]}}</ref>

In July 2010, it was reported that Kosar was on the verge of losing property in [[Geauga County, Ohio]] for unpaid back taxes totaling $173,557.90.<ref>{{cite news | title=Diminishing tax payments by former Cleveland Brown | url=http://gcm.php.mediaspanonline.com/article.php?sid=3504 | access-date=October 17, 2011 | work=Geauga County Maple Leaf | date=July 15, 2010 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120425073745/http://gcm.php.mediaspanonline.com/article.php?sid=3504 | archive-date=April 25, 2012}}</ref> In September 2010, the trustees of [[Auburn Township, Geauga County, Ohio|Auburn Township]] indicated it was considering purchasing the land in [[foreclosure]].<ref>{{cite news | last=Ryder | first=Diane | title=Auburn may buy Bernie Kosar's property | url=http://www.news-herald.com/articles/2010/09/22/news/nh3067073.txt?viewmode=fullstory | archive-url=https://archive.today/20120912092709/http://www.news-herald.com/articles/2010/09/22/news/nh3067073.txt?viewmode=fullstory | url-status=dead | archive-date=September 12, 2012 | access-date=October 17, 2011 | newspaper=The News-Herald | location=[[Willoughby, Ohio]] | date=September 22, 2010 }}</ref>

Kosar has lent his name to Kosar's Wood-Fired Grill at the [[MGM Northfield Park|Hard Rock Rock Casino Northfield Park]] in [[Northfield, Ohio]], which opened in December 2013.<ref>{{cite news | title=Bernie Kosar lends his name to Northfield Park restaurant | url=https://www.cleveland.com/metro/2013/08/bernie_kosar_lends_his_name_to.html | first=Thomas | last=Ott | work=The Plain Dealer | location=Cleveland, Ohio | date=August 22, 2013 | access-date=December 30, 2021}}</ref>

Kosar has teamed with Ohio grocery chain [[Heinen's Fine Foods|Heinen's]] for a motivational and wellness seminar series based on Kosar's autobiography, ''Learning to Scramble'',<ref>[https://www.geaugamapleleaf.com/news/former-beloved-browns-quarterback-learns-to-scramble-off-field/ "Former Beloved Brown’s Quarterback Learns ‘to Scramble’ Off Field"] by Rose Nemunaitis ''Geauga County Maple Leaf'' (July 19, 2018). Retrieved December 7, 2019</ref> which he published in 2017.<ref>[https://www.clevelandlandmarkspress.com/book_details.php?bid=27#&panel1-1 ''Learning to Scramble'' by Bernie Kosar with Craig Stout] ''clevelandlandmarkspress.com''. Retrieved December 7, 2019</ref>

In October 2023, Kosar announced a line of wellness products named U Matter Wellness Essentials<ref>{{cite web|url=https://x.com/BernieKosarQB/status/1714335992268611900|title=U Matter Wellness Essentials announcement on X|date=October 17, 2023}}</ref> under his Kosar Wellness brand, selling supplements including digestive enzymes, fermented vegetable powder and [[Effervescence|effervescent]] [[Humic substance|humic fulvic acid]] tablets.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://kosarwellness.com/ | title=U Matter Wellness Essentials official website | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231130113916/https://kosarwellness.com/|archive-date=November 30, 2023}}</ref> As part of the product launch, Kosar partnered with Foundation Health Solutions, an Ohio-based [[long-term care]] company.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dcKvEhr-Mi0 | title=U Matter Wellness Essentials and Foundations Health Solutions partnership| website=[[YouTube]]| date=November 21, 2023}}</ref> In 2023 Kosar was involved in a lawsuit related to Kosar Wellness.<ref name=pd20241202/>

A Jan. 5, 2024, Cleveland.com story{{full citation needed|date=December 2024}} by Peter Chakerian stated that Bernie Kosar just launched a new patented coffee blend, designed by Kosar himself to "boost immunity, protect against chronic diseases and strengthen heart health."

==Personal life==
On June 22, 1990, Kosar married Babette Ferre<ref>[https://www.nndb.com/people/962/000163473/ Bernie Kosar] ''[[NNDB]]'' Retrieved December 5, 2019.</ref> whom he first met as a [[University of Miami]] student.<ref>[https://www.si.com/vault/1988/08/29/118269/brainy-brown-bernie-kosars-bad-body-and-sidearm-delivery-make-coaches-wince-but-his-quick-mind-has-opponents-of-the-browns-feeling-blue "Brainy Brown"] by [[Rick Telander]] ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'' (August 29, 1988). Retrieved December 5, 2019.</ref> They had four children. Ferre filed for divorce in 2005, alleging that Kosar had engaged in reckless spending, bad investments, and drug use. The divorce was finalized in 2007.<ref>[https://bauerfamilylaw.blogspot.com/2007/04/ "Babette vs. Bernie: Battling Over Bucks"] by Joan Fleischman ''bauerfamilylaw'' (April 18, 2007) via ''[[Miami Herald]]'' (link broken). Retrieved December 5, 2019.</ref> Kosar dated Tami Longaberger of [[The Longaberger Company]] from 2009 to 2013.<ref>[https://www.cleveland.com/pluto/blog/2010/08/in_second_half_of_his_life_for.html "In Second Half of His Life, Former Cleveland Browns Quarterback Bernie Kosar Begins a Comeback"] by [[Terry Pluto]] (August 14, 2010) ''cleveland.com''. Retrieved December 5, 2019.</ref>

Kosar was prominently featured in ''Broke'', a 2012 [[ESPN]] ''[[30 For 30]]'' documentary about the financial problems common among high-earning athletes. According to one review of ''Broke'', "[Kosar's] story proved to be the true heart of the film" with Kosar's upfront discussion of family problems and bad business decisions.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Conway |first1=Tyler |title=Bernie Kosar: Former QB Exposes Pitfalls of Athletes Trusting Family in 'Broke' |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/1357277-bernie-kosar-former-qb-exposes-pitfalls-of-athletes-trusting-family-in-broke |website=Bleacher Report |access-date=December 30, 2021 |date=October 3, 2012}}</ref>

On September 29, 2013, Kosar was pulled over by law enforcement in [[Solon, Ohio]] for speeding and was arrested on suspicion of [[driving under the influence]] of alcohol. He later pleaded no contest to a lesser charge of reckless operation and received a $750 fine and suspended jail sentence.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nfl/2014/04/28/bernie-kosar-browns-reckless-operation-charge-plea-drunken-driving/8421997 | title=Bernie Kosar pleads no contest to reckless operation charge | work=USA Today | agency=Associated Press | date=April 28, 2014 | access-date=October 26, 2018}}</ref>

Kosar's political views are undetermined, but was invited to the [[2016 Republican National Convention]], and spoke positively of host state Ohio and host city [[Cleveland, Ohio|Cleveland]] in the context of the Convention being held there.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Borchardt |first1=Jackie |title=Former Browns QB Bernie Kosar mingles with Ohio GOP delegates at RNC |url=https://www.cleveland.com/rnc-2016/2016/07/former_browns_qb_bernie_kosar.html |website=Cleveland.com |access-date=30 October 2022 |date=18 July 2016}}</ref> In [[2022 United States Senate election in Ohio|2022]], he appeared in an advertisement for [[Tim Ryan (Ohio politician)|Tim Ryan]], the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate in [[2022 United States Senate election in Ohio|Ohio]].<ref>{{Cite tweet |last=Ryan |first=Tim |user=TimRyan |number=1585310334273089536 |date=26 October 2022 |title=Thank you @BernieKosarQB—this November, Ohioans are going to reject extremism and elect a leader for all Ohioans.|access-date=30 October 2022}}</ref>

===Health===
Kosar continues to deal with lingering health issues related to several [[concussion]]s he sustained during his playing career and enrolled in a treatment program to alleviate his symptoms.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://proplayerinsiders.com/nfl-player-team-news-features/bernie-kosar-is-undergoing-groundbreaking-treatment-for-brain-trauma/ | title=Bernie Kosar is Undergoing "Groundbreaking" Treatment for Brain Trauma | first=Joey | last=Rivaldo | website=ProPlayerInsiders.com | date=January 10, 2013 | access-date=October 26, 2018 | archive-date=September 2, 2018 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180902011835/http://proplayerinsiders.com/nfl-player-team-news-features/bernie-kosar-is-undergoing-groundbreaking-treatment-for-brain-trauma/ | url-status=dead }}</ref> Kosar says the experimental treatment has been helpful and has promoted it to other players who may have developed symptoms related to [[chronic traumatic encephalopathy]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/8833397/bernie-kosar-former-cleveland-browns-quarterback-finding-help-concussions | title=Bernie Kosar happy to find treatment | website=ESPN.com | agency=Associated Press | date=January 11, 2013 | access-date=October 26, 2018}}</ref> For over a decade, Kosar's symptoms have included insomnia, slurred speech, and ringing in his head.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.cleveland.com/browns/2013/01/former_cleveland_browns_quarte_2.html | title=Former Cleveland Browns quarterback Bernie Kosar receiving 'groundbreaking' treatments for brain trauma | first=Tom | last=Reed | work=The Plain Dealer | location=Cleveland, Ohio | date=January 10, 2013 | access-date=December 30, 2021}}</ref>

In 2024, Kosar said he was diagnosed with [[Cirrhosis|cirrhosis of the liver]] and early symptoms of [[Parkinson's disease]].<ref>{{cite news|first1=Dennis|last1=Manoloff|first2=Dillon|last2=Stewart|title=Exclusive: Bernie Kosar Upbeat While Facing a Liver Transplant and Early Signs of Parkinson's|url=https://clevelandmagazine.com/in-the-cle/people/articles/bernie-kosar-facing-liver-transplant-early-parkinsons|work=[[Cleveland Magazine]]|date=July 9, 2024|access-date=July 10, 2024}}</ref> On November 17, 2025, he received a [[Liver transplantation|liver transplant]].<ref>{{cite news|first1=Dave|last1=DeNatale|first2=Anna|last2=Meyer|first3=Monica|last3=Robins|first4=Ryan|last4=Haidet|first5=Chris|last5=Beeble|title='I'm out and I'm feeling good': Cleveland Browns legend Bernie Kosar posts message after undergoing liver transplant|url=https://www.wkyc.com/article/sports/nfl/browns/bernie-kosar-cleveland-browns-liver-transplant-surgery-university-hospitals-update/95-6acdcd7b-1ebb-410b-8f5d-7e3ea129350a|publisher=[[WKYC|WKYC-TV]]|date=November 17, 2025|access-date=November 17, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|first=Terry|last=Pluto|title=Bernie Kosar has successful liver transplant, is grateful for support of fans & the Browns, friend says|url=https://www.cleveland.com/browns/2025/11/bernie-kosar-has-successful-liver-transplant-grateful-for-support-of-fans-browns-terry-pluto.html|work=The Plain Dealer|date=November 17, 2025|access-date=November 19, 2025}}</ref>

Parmalee''' (born September 16, 1967) is an American [[American football|football]] coach and former [[running back]] who is the [[running backs coach]] for the [[Carolina Panthers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He previously served as the running backs coach for the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] from 2021 to 2023 and also served as an assistant coach for [[Oakland Raiders]], [[Kansas City Chiefs]] and [[Miami Dolphins]]. Parmalee played [[college football]] for the [[Ball State Cardinals football|Ball State Cardinals]], where he was inducted into the Hall of Fame in 2001, and was signed by the [[Miami Dolphins]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 1992. Playing for nine seasons in the NFL, Parmalee also played for the [[New York Jets]]. ==Playing career== Parmalee played high school football at [[Lincoln High School (New Jersey)|Lincoln High School]] in [[Jersey City, New Jersey]].{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20070517130828/http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=PARMABER01 Bernie Parmalee]}}, Database Football. Accessed January 3, 2008. Parmalee played in college at Ball State University, where he is the 3rd leading rusher all-time and was named MAC Freshman of the Year in 1987. {{NFL predraft | height ft = 5 | height in = 11 1/8 | weight = 191 | dash = 4.80 | ten split = 1.81 | twenty split = 2.86 | shuttle = 4.23 | vertical = 28.5 | broad ft = 9 | broad in = 11 | bench = 11 | arm span = 33 | hand span = 9 1/4 | note = All values from [[NFL Combine]]{{Cite web |url=https://nflcombineresults.com/playerpage.php?f=Bernie&l=Parmalee&i=25140 |title=Bernie Parmalee Combine Results |website=NFLCombineResults.com |access-date=June 1, 2026}} }} Parmalee played running back for the [[Miami Dolphins]] and the [[New York Jets]] from 1992 to 2000. Parmalee's professional opportunity came when he tried out for the [[Miami Dolphins]] after working for [[United Parcel Service|UPS]]. He played seven seasons with the Dolphins (1992–98) in 104 games, scoring fifteen rushing touchdowns and three receiving touchdowns while rushing for 1,959 yards and amassing 1,306 receiving yards. In 1999, he went to the Jets and played two seasons in 30 games with two rushing touchdowns, 220 rushing yards, and 179 receiving yards. ==Coaching career== ===Miami Dolphins=== Parmalee coached both [[special teams]] and [[tight end]]s for the [[Miami Dolphins]] from 2002 to 2004. ===Notre Dame Fighting Irish=== Parmalee coached both special teams and tight ends for the Notre Dame Fighting Irish from 2005 to 2009. Irish tight ends did well under Parmalee's tutelage having produced multiple [[John Mackey Award]] finalists during his tenure ([[Anthony Fasano]] and [[John Carlson (Football)|John Carlson]]). ===Kansas City Chiefs=== The Chiefs announced him as their Tight Ends coach on February 1, 2010.[http://www.kcchiefs.com/news/2010/02/01/chiefs_finalize_coaching_staff_with_parmalee_smith_and_thomas/ Chiefs Finalize Coaching Staff] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100204090555/http://www.kcchiefs.com/news/2010/02/01/chiefs_finalize_coaching_staff_with_parmalee_smith_and_thomas/ |date=February 4, 2010 }} ===Oakland Raiders=== He was hired by the Raiders as their new running backs coach on January 25, 2015. In Parmalee's first season in Oakland, [[Latavius Murray]] made the Pro Bowl, running for 1066 yards — the team's first 1000-yard rusher in five years. In Parmalee's second season in Oakland, the Raiders had the league's 6th ranked rushing attack. As [[Jon Gruden]] took over as head coach of the Raiders after the 2017 season, Parmalee was ousted with most of the Raiders coaching staff.{{Cite web|url=https://www.silverandblackpride.com/2018/2/13/17011066/former-raiders-running-backs-coach-bernie-parmalee-to-take-same-position-with-falcons|title = Former Raiders running backs coach Bernie Parmalee to take same position with Falcons|date = February 13, 2018}} ===Atlanta Falcons=== In 2018, Parmalee was hired to be the running backs coach for the Falcons. He coached [[Ito Smith]] in his first season where he tallied four rushing touchdowns, the most rushing touchdowns by a Falcons rookie since 2002.{{cite web|url=https://www.atlantafalcons.com/team/coaches-roster/bernie-parmalee|title=Bernie Parmalee|work=[[Atlanta Falcons]]|accessdate=November 4, 2019}} After working as an offensive assistant and assistant special teams coach to start the 2019 season, he returned to being the running backs coach on November 4.{{cite web|last=McFadden|first=Will|url=https://www.atlantafalcons.com/news/falcons-announce-trio-of-coaching-changes|title=Falcons announce trio of coaching changes|publisher=[[Atlanta Falcons]]|date=November 4, 2019|accessdate=November 4, 2019|archive-date=November 4, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191104181142/https://www.atlantafalcons.com/news/falcons-announce-trio-of-coaching-changes|url-status=dead}} On October 12, 2020, Parmalee was shifted from running backs coach to special teams coordinator, as part of a midseason shakeup of the coaching staff. ===Jacksonville Jaguars=== On February 10, 2021, Parmalee was hired by the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] as their running backs coach under head coach [[Urban Meyer]]. '''Bertram Hays Jones''' (born September 7, 1951) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[quarterback]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 10 seasons with the [[Baltimore Colts]] and [[Los Angeles Rams]]. He was named the [[NFL Most Valuable Player]] in 1976 with the Colts.

Jones played [[college football]] for the [[LSU Tigers football|LSU Tigers]], earning consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors in 1972. He was selected by the Colts in the first round of the [[1973 NFL draft]] with the second overall pick. He is the son of former NFL [[running back]] [[Dub Jones (American football)|Dub Jones]] of the [[Cleveland Browns]]. In 2016, Jones was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]].

==Biography==
===Early life===

Bert Jones was born on September 7, 1951, in [[Ruston, Louisiana]]. His father, [[Dub Jones (American football)|Dub Jones]], was a [[halfback (gridiron football)|halfback]] who played for ten years in the [[All-America Football Conference]] (AAFC) and [[National Football League]] (NFL).

He attended [[Ruston High School]], where he was given the nickname "the Ruston Rifle".

===College===

Jones attended [[Louisiana State University]] (LSU) in [[Baton Rouge, Louisiana]], where he played for the [[LSU Tigers football|Tigers]]. While at LSU, Jones only [[Starting lineup|started]] two games prior to the end of his junior year, but he started every game thereafter, leading LSU to a 12–2–1 record.

In 1971, Jones threw for 945 yards with nine [[touchdown]]s and four [[interception]]s while splitting time with Paul Lyons. Against the wishes of LSU fans, Jones was forced to share quarterback duties with Lyons because of Jones's bickering with head coach [[Charlie McClendon]] over signal calling.<ref>Chet Hilburn, ''The Mystique of Tiger Stadium: 25 Greatest Games: The Ascension of LSU Football'' (Bloomington, Indiana: WestBow Press, 2012), p. 44.</ref> Lyons himself threw for over 800 yards and 11 touchdowns that year.

In 1972 after taking over at quarterback, Jones threw for 1,446 yards with 14 touchdowns and seven interceptions on 199 pass attempts. Except for one week, LSU spent the entire season ranked in the [[Associated Press|AP]] Top 10. One of Jones's most famous moments came in the 1972 LSU vs. Ole Miss game, when he led LSU to a 17–16 last-second victory by hitting running back Brad Davis in the [[end zone]] for a touchdown as time expired. After the season, Jones became the first quarterback in LSU history to be awarded consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-America]] honors.<ref name=Houma>{{cite news|title=LSU to honor Bert Jones at Saturday's game|url=http://www.houmatoday.com/sports/20161020/lsu-to-honor-bert-jones-at-saturdays-game|access-date=December 11, 2016|work=The Houma Courier|date=October 20, 2016}}</ref> Jones also finished fourth in the vote for the [[Heisman Trophy]] and was named the national collegiate Player of the Year by ''[[The Sporting News]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sportingnews.com/archives/almanac/nfl/cfbplay.html |title=Sporting News Archives |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010121215500/http://sportingnews.com/archives/almanac/nfl/cfbplay.html |archive-date=January 21, 2001 }} Retrieved March 27, 2009.</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Tigers and Vols Break for Xmas|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/8685977/tigers_and_vols_break_for_xmas/|access-date=February 1, 2017|work=The Town Talk|date=December 21, 1972|page=11}}</ref>

During his 17 games at LSU, Jones completed 52.6 percent of his passes for 3,225 yards and 28 touchdowns, which at the time was the most career passing yards and touchdowns of any quarterback in school history.<ref name=Houma/>

In 2016, Jones was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{cite web|first=Ron|last=Higgins|date=January 8, 2016|title=Former LSU quarterback Bert Jones elected to College Football Hall of Fame|work=The Times-Picayune|url=http://www.nola.com/lsu/index.ssf/2016/01/former_lsu_quarterback_bert_jo.html|access-date=December 7, 2016}}</ref>

===Professional career===
Jones was projected by NFL scouts to be the first quarterback drafted in [[1973 NFL Draft|1973]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Mizell|first=Hubert|title=Pro Scouts Look To Jones, Butz As Best|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=ehgfAAAAIBAJ&pg=6238%2C3870396|access-date=December 31, 2016|work=The Tuscaloosa News|agency=Associated Press|date=December 20, 1972|page=19}}</ref> He was chosen second overall by the Baltimore Colts to be the Colts' heir apparent to [[Johnny Unitas]], who was later traded to San Diego. His debut came on September 16, 1973, in a loss to the Cleveland Browns. During his eight-year tenure as the Colts' starting quarterback, Jones and his teammates enjoyed three consecutive [[AFC East]] division titles (1975–77). But in each of those years, the Colts lost in the first round of the playoffs. The 1977 playoff game (known as [[Ghost to the Post]]) is famous as the fourth longest game in NFL history; the Colts fell to the [[Oakland Raiders]], 37–31. Jones missed most of 1978 and 1979 with a shoulder injury, and the Colts fell to last place in the AFC East those two seasons.

The 1976 regular season was Jones' finest as a professional; he threw for 3,104 yards and a career-high 24 [[touchdown]]s, compiling a passer rating of 102.5. He was one of only three quarterbacks to achieve a 100+ [[passer rating]] during the entire decade of the 1970s, joining [[Dallas Cowboys|Dallas]]' [[Roger Staubach]] (1971) and Oakland's [[Ken Stabler]] (1976). Jones was honored by the [[Associated Press]] as 1976's [[AP NFL Most Valuable Player Award|NFL Most Valuable Player]]<ref>{{cite news|title=Colts' Jones most valuable|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/8682560/colts_jones_most_valuable/|access-date=February 1, 2017|work=Reno Gazette-Journal|agency=Associated Press|date=December 30, 1976|page=14|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> and [[NFL Offensive Player of the Year Award|NFL Offensive Player of the Year]],<ref>{{cite news|title=Offensive Award to Bert Jones|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=861&dat=19761230&id=YAJaAAAAIBAJ&pg=7016,6587720&hl=en|access-date=July 5, 2016|work=The Victoria Advocate|agency=Associated Press|date=December 30, 1976|page=1B}}</ref> selected first-team All-Pro,<ref>{{cite news|title=Bert Jones Quarterbacks All-Pro Squad|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/8682770/bert_jones_quarterbacks_allpro_squad/|access-date=February 1, 2017|work=Beckley Post-Herald|agency=Associated Press|date=December 28, 1976|page=7}}</ref> and named to the [[Pro Bowl]] team. He was also selected second-team All-Pro following the 1977 season.

The remainder of Jones' playing career beyond 1977 was curtailed by several injuries, the first of which was a [[separated shoulder]] after a hit from [[Al Baker]] in the Colts' 13–7 win over the [[Detroit Lions]] at the [[Pontiac Silverdome]] on August 26, 1978, in the final preseason contest for both teams.<ref>[https://www.delcotimes.com/sports/grotz-preseason-nfl-games-can-do-more-harm-than-good/article_32071792-b897-11e9-83be-7fca0ae7a0f5.html Grotz, Bob. "Preseason NFL games can do more harm than good," ''Delaware County Daily Times'' (Swarthmore, PA ), Wednesday, August 7, 2019.] Retrieved October 19, 2020</ref>

During an October 26, 1980 game against the [[St. Louis Cardinals (football team)|St. Louis Cardinals]], Jones made NFL history when he was sacked a record 12 times. This broke the record at the time held by many quarterbacks, including Jones's then back-up, [[Greg Landry]], who had been sacked 11 times while he was a member of the [[Detroit Lions]] in a game against the [[Dallas Cowboys]] on October 6, 1975.<ref>NFL Record and Fact Book {{ISBN|978-1-60320-833-8}}</ref>

In 1982, his final season, Jones played in four games for the Los Angeles Rams before a neck injury forced him to retire.<ref>{{cite news|title=Bert Jones retires due to neck injury|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/13134992/bert_jones_retires_due_to_neck_injury/|access-date=August 16, 2017|work=New Braunfels Herald-Zeitung|agency=Associated Press|date=May 20, 1983|page=6|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

In 1990, Jones participated in the first NFL Quarterback Challenge. He finished first in the retiree category and third in the regular competition (The regular competition taking the top three finishers from the alumni competition and adding them to the regular field of current quarterbacks). Given his strong performance, [[Bobby Beathard]], then the general manager of the Chargers, wanted Jones to come out of retirement,<ref>{{cite news|title=Beathard Interested in Bert Jones's Return|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1990/06/20/beathard-interested-in-bert-joness-return/eb153c93-691b-4281-93ed-0661b15ac1fd/|access-date=August 16, 2017|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=June 20, 1990}}</ref> but Jones was 38 at the time and chose not to try a comeback.

Longtime scout [[Ernie Accorsi]] is quoted as saying that if Bert Jones had played under different circumstances, he probably would have been the greatest player ever. [[John Riggins]] has been quoted as saying Jones was the toughest competitor he has ever witnessed.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/87398-baltimore-colts-forgotten-hero-bert-jones |title=Baltimore Colts' Forgotten Hero Bert Jones |first=Chad |last=Lamas |date=November 30, 2008 |work=Bleacher Report}}</ref> On the eve of [[Super Bowl XLII]], New England Patriots head coach [[Bill Belichick]], in discussing his choices for the greatest quarterbacks of all time, described Jones as the best "pure passer" he had ever seen.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/08033/854261-66.stm |title=Super Bowl Notebook: Belichick lists Bert Jones as one of his all-time QBs |work=Pittsburgh Post Gazette |first=Gene |last=Collier |date=February 2, 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220809043751/https://old.post-gazette.com/pg/08033/854261-66.stm |archive-date=August 9, 2022 |access-date=October 21, 2023}}</ref>

In 2022, the [[Professional Football Researchers Association]] named Jones to the [[PFRA Hall of Very Good]] Class of 2022.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://profootballresearchers.com/hall-of-very-good-2022.html |title= PFRA's Hall of Very Good Class of 2022 |author=Professional Football Researchers Association|access-date=July 19, 2022}}</ref>

'''Bhawoh Papi Jue''' ({{IPAc-en|ˌ|b|aʊ|_|ˈ|dʒ|uː}}; born May 24, 1979) is a Liberian former professional [[American football]] [[Safety (American football position)|safety]]. He was originally selected by the [[Green Bay Packers]] in the third round of the [[2001 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Penn State Nittany Lions football|Penn State Nittany Lions]].

He was also a member of the [[San Diego Chargers]], [[St. Louis Rams]], [[Arizona Cardinals]], and [[Florida Tuskers]]. He is distinguished as being the first [[Liberian people|Liberian]] to play in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

==Early life==
Jue and his mother immigrated from [[Liberia]] to the US when he was a year old. He lived in [[California]] and [[Rhode Island]] before settling in Virginia.

Jue attended [[Chantilly High School]] in [[Chantilly, Virginia]], where he was a two-sport letterman in [[American football]] and [[basketball]]. He also ran [[track and field]]. As a senior, he helped lead Chantilly to the 1996 Virginia State AAA Football title, making 73 tackles and 3 [[interception]]s as a [[defensive back]] and rushing for over 1,200 yards and 21 [[touchdown]]s as a [[Halfback (American football)|tailback]]. That year, he was named a [[USA Today]] [[All-America]] selection, and [[Associated Press]] first-team All-State on both offense and defense. He also earned Region Defensive Player of the Year, and Conference Player of the Year.

==College career==
Jue attended [[Penn State University]], from 1997 to 2001. He finished his career there with 99 [[tackle (football move)|tackles]], 7 [[interception]]s and 28 passes defended. As the [[Nittany Lion|Nittany Lion's]] starting left [[cornerback]], he was named Honorable Mention [[List of All-Big Ten Conference football teams|All-Big Ten]] in 2000 and was selected to play in the 2001 [[Senior Bowl]]. During his college career, he also played in the [[Alamo Bowl]] and the [[Outback Bowl]]. Jue was roommates with three other future NFLers at Penn State: [[Omar Easy]], [[John Gilmore (American football)|John Gilmore]] and [[Tony Stewart (American football)|Tony Stewart]].

==NFL career==

===2001 NFL draft===
Jue was selected with the 71st pick in the third round of the [[2001 NFL draft]] by the Green Bay Packers after his college career.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2001 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2001/draft.htm |access-date=18 March 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

===Green Bay Packers===
Jue began the season switching between cornerback and safety, but was eventually permanently placed as a safety when he took over for the injured [[LeRoy Butler]] midway through the season. He totaled forty-six tackles with two interceptions, and was named the Packers' Defensive Rookie of the Year. His sophomore season was limited to four games after suffering various injuries that put him on injured reserve early in the year. In 2003, he played in all games, primarily on special teams and had a career best 1.5 sacks, coupled with twenty-seven solo tackles. The following season saw him make forty-two tackles with an interception.

===San Diego Chargers===
After the 2004 season, Jue left to sign with the San Diego Chargers. He set new career highs with forty-seven tackles and three interceptions. He spent most of the 2006 season as a reserve due to injury. On 1 September 2007, they released him.

===St. Louis Rams===
On 10 October 2007, Jue signed with the [[St. Louis Rams]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pasquarelli |first=Len |author-link=Len Pasquarelli |date=2007-10-10 |title=Hurting at safety, Rams bring in ex-Charger Jue |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3056869 |access-date=2025-07-14 |website=ESPN.com}}</ref> He was cut by the St. Louis Rams on 6 November 2007.

'''William Ernest Bain''' (born August 9, 1952) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive lineman]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[USC Trojans football|USC Trojans]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Bill Bain Career Stats|url=https://www.nfl.com/players/bill-bain/stats/career|access-date=2021-07-25|website=NFL.com|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Early life==
Bain attended [[St. Paul High School (Santa Fe Springs, California)|St. Paul High School]], where he played for coach [[Marijon Ancich]].

==College career==
Bain played [[college football]] at the [[University of Southern California]] and was an [[All-America]] offensive lineman in 1974.  Bain also played at [[University of Colorado at Boulder|University of Colorado]] and [[San Diego City College]].

==Professional career==
Bain played 11 seasons in the NFL. He played for the [[Green Bay Packers]] (1975), the [[Denver Broncos]] (1976, 1978), the [[Los Angeles Rams]]<ref>{{cite web |last1=Roberts |first1=Rich |title=It Has Been a Strain, Says Bain; No Longer Can He Carry Around 300 Pounds |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-10-15-sp-16322-story.html |website=Los Angeles Times |date=15 October 1985 |access-date=23 July 2021}}</ref> (1979–1985), the [[New England Patriots]] (1986), and the [[New York Jets]] (1986).<ref name=":0" />

==Personal life==
Bain and his wife, Elizabeth (Liz), have four daughters: Jennifer, Kristen, Anne (Annie), Elizabeth (Bitty). He has two grandchildren: William and Christopher. He currently resides in [[East Greenwich, RI]].

'''William Frederick Bates''' (born June 6, 1961) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who spent his entire 15-year career as a [[Safety (American football position)|safety]] for the [[Dallas Cowboys]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  A fan favorite, he was a [[Pro Bowl]] selection in 1984, played in [[Super Bowl XXVIII]] and [[Super Bowl XXX]], and was on the Cowboys' roster for [[Super Bowl XXVII]].  He played [[college football]] for the [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Tennessee Volunteers]].

==Early life==
Bates attended [[Farragut High School]] in [[Farragut, Tennessee]], where he played under rising head coach [[Ken Sparks]].  He recorded over 1,000 return yards, 14 interceptions, and nearly 200 tackles during his high school career where he was known for his hard hitting tackles.<ref name=1979guide>''[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=740&pg=58 1979 Tennessee Volunteers Football Program] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304041130/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=740&pg=58 |date=March 4, 2016 }}'' (University of Tennessee, 1979), p. 56. Retrieved: July 3, 2013.</ref>

He helped lead the Admirals to the state semi-finals in 1978, in which the Admirals lost to Red Bank by one point. He was all-state in football and [[basketball]] his senior year. He also practiced [[track and field]]. He was considered the 4th best high school recruit in the state in football.<ref name=1979guide />

==College career==
Bates played college football at the [[University of Tennessee]] from 1979 through the 1982 season, where he was a four-year starter, the first two at [[free safety]] and the last two at [[strong safety]].  As a freshman in 1979, he registered 55 tackles (35 solo), 3 sacks, an interception, and 2 fumble recoveries.  In 1980, he had 43 tackles (24 solo), including 3 tackles for a loss, to go along with an interception and 2 fumble recoveries. In 1981, he tallied 71 tackles (48 solo) and a team-leading 4 interceptions.  During his senior year in 1982, he registered 86 tackles (61 solo), including 2 tackles for a loss, and 3 interceptions.<ref>[http://www.utsports.com/sports/m-footbl/fball-stats/b.htm Tennessee Career Football Statistics] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131031163456/http://www.utsports.com/sports/m-footbl/fball-stats/b.htm |date=October 31, 2013 }}, UTSports.com.  Retrieved: July 3, 2013.</ref>

On October 20, 1979, Bates recorded 8 tackles, a sack, and 2 fumble recoveries against [[1979 Alabama Crimson Tide football team|Alabama]], who were ranked number one and would go on to win the national championship that year.<ref>''[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=741&pg=40 1980 Tennessee Volunteers Football Program] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304094244/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=741&pg=40 |date=March 4, 2016 }}'' (University of Tennessee, 1980), p. 38.</ref>  At the end of 1979 he was honored by being named to the Freshman [[All-America]]n team. He also won the team's "hardest hitter" award on several occasions throughout his career. He was named second-team [[List of All-SEC football teams|All-SEC]] as a junior and senior.

During Tennessee's 16–15 loss to eventual national champion [[1980 Georgia Bulldogs football team|Georgia]] on September 6, 1980, Georgia running back [[Herschel Walker]] and Bates met on the 5-yard line in a play that still lives in many college football highlights. Walker ran over Bates to score the first touchdown of his college career.<ref name=hix>Tim Hix, "[http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=226&pg=51&catid=49&s=bates Vol Profile: Bill Bates] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304054838/http://diglib.lib.utk.edu/fbpro/main.php?bid=226&pg=51&catid=49&s=bates |date=March 4, 2016 }}," ''Tennessee vs. Washington State Football Program'' (University of Tennessee, 1982), pp. 47–48.</ref><ref name="Freshman">{{Cite news |last=Schlabach |first=Mark |author-link=Mark Schlabach |date=October 8, 2015 |title=From The Mag: That time Herschel Walker trucked Bill Bates |url=http://www.espn.com/espn/feature/story/_/id/13829698/when-georgia-herschel-walker-ran-tennessee-bill-bates-oral-history |access-date=September 10, 2017 |work=ESPN.com}}</ref> The two would later become teammates for several seasons with the [[Dallas Cowboys]].<ref name=Freshman/>

In 2021, he was  inducted into the Tennessee Sports Hall of Fame.

==Professional career==
Bates went undrafted in the [[1983 NFL draft]] after he ran the 40-yard dash in a disappointing 4.8 seconds during the [[NFL Scouting Combine]]. He was selected by the [[New Jersey Generals]] in the [[1983 USFL Territorial Draft]], but he decided to sign as an undrafted free agent with the [[Dallas Cowboys]], which had been his favorite team growing up. He was a long shot to make the team but he earned a roster spot. From the start he excelled on [[special teams]], being named [[NFL]] special teams player of the year and to the NFL All-rookie team. He started in the regular-season against the [[Seattle Seahawks]] in the playoffs against the [[Los Angeles Rams]] at [[strong safety]], replacing an injured [[Dextor Clinkscale]]. He also played as a linebacker in the Cowboys' "4–0" pass defense, posting 84 tackles (seventh on the team), one interception, 4 passes defensed, 4 sacks, one forced fumble and 2 fumble recoveries.

In [[1984 NFL season|1984]], he missed 4 games after being placed on the [[injured reserve list]], because of a preseason injury suffered against the [[Green Bay Packers]]. He was named the team's special teams captain. He started against the [[Indianapolis Colts]] at strong safety, making a team-high 7 tackles, one sack, one interception, one pass defensed and one fumble recovery. He started against the [[Washington Redskins]] at [[outside linebacker]]. He led the team with 10 defensive tackles in the season finale against the [[Miami Dolphins]]. He played as a linebacker in the team's "4–0" pass defense. He posted 52 defensive tackles, one interception and one fumble recovery. He set a club record for [[defensive back]]s with 5 sacks. He was selected to the [[Pro Bowl]] in just his second year, after influencing the NFL to create a first-time roster spot for special teams players that were non-returners, making Bates the first such player to receive that honor. He was named [[All-Pro]] and [[NFL]] special teams player of the year.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Rick Gosselin's all-time NFL Special Teams Unit|url=https://www.si.com/nfl/talkoffame/nfl/rick-gosselin-s-all-time-nfl-special-teams-unit|access-date=January 7, 2022|website=Sports Illustrated}}</ref>

In [[1985 NFL season|1985]], he was used as a punt returner out of necessity, registering 22 returns for 152 yards (6.9-yard avg.). He also had 51 defensive tackles, 4 interceptions and one sack. He started 2 games at strong safety.

In [[1986 NFL season|1986]], he became a starter at strong safety and remained there until [[1988 NFL season|1988]], after which he was used only in the [[Nickel defense]] packages. At the end of the [[1989 NFL season|1989 season]], [[Jimmy Johnson (American football coach)|Jimmy Johnson]] informed Bates that he was going to be left unprotected on the team's [[Plan B free agency]] list. Although the [[Minnesota Vikings]] were interested in him, just before the deadline, the Cowboys decided to protect him.

In [[1989 NFL season|1989]], he was the leader in special teams tackles with 19. The next year, he led the team again with 23 tackles, becoming the first player in franchise history to do it in consecutive years.

Bates received the team's [[Bob Lilly]] Award four consecutive seasons from [[1990 NFL season|1990]] to [[1994 NFL season|1994]]. This award is selected by a vote of the fans and annually goes to the Cowboy player who displays leadership and character on and off the field. In [[1992 NFL season|1992]], he suffered a season-ending knee injury.  After the [[1993 NFL season|1993 season]], he was selected by his teammates to receive the [[Ed Block Courage Award]] for successfully overcoming his injury and leading the team in special teams tackles (25).

Upon his retirement after the [[1997 NFL season|1997 season]], he was considered one of the most beloved Cowboys of all time. Over his 15-year career, he had 14 interceptions and 122 return yards.

Bates earned three Super Bowl rings with the Cowboys, playing in [[Super Bowl XXVIII]] and [[Super Bowl XXX]]. He was on injured reserve during the [[1992 NFL season|1992 season]], when the Cowboys played in [[Super Bowl XXVII]], due to a knee injury.

[[Tom Landry]] once said, “If we had 11 players on the field who played as hard as Bill Bates does and did their homework like he does, we’d be almost impossible to beat”.<ref>{{Cite web|title=ESPN 50 Greatest Dallas Cowboys|url=http://www.espn.com/dallas/photos/gallery/_/id/7356790/image/3/49-bill-bates-50-greatest-cowboys|access-date=January 7, 2022|website=Premiere Speakers Bureau}}</ref> He described Bates (Real Kill) and [[Cliff Harris]] (Captain Crash) as "the hardest hitters I ever saw."<ref name=amazon>[https://www.amazon.com/SHOOT-STAR-Bill-Bates-ebook/dp/B006MGTN0E/ref=sr_1_1?keywords=Shoot+for+the+Star&qid=1670540845&sr=8-1 Editorial Review for ''Shoot for the Star''], Amazon.com.  Retrieved: July 3, 2013.</ref>  Referring to Bates's reputation as a hard hitter, [[John Madden]] stated, "Every game starts with a kick. With Bill Bates on the field, every game begins with a ''bang''!"<ref name=amazon />

==Personal life==
After his retirement as a player following the 1997 season, Bill was an assistant coach for the Cowboys for five years under head coaches Chan Gailey and Dave Campo.  In 2003, Bill spent a year as special teams coach under head coach and former Cowboy linebacker Jack Del Rio.  Beginning in 2004, he coached football at his sons' high schools, Nease High School and Ponte Vedra High School in Ponte Vedra Beach, FL.<ref name="premiere">{{Cite web|title=Bill Bates Bio|url=https://premierespeakers.com/bill-bates/bio|access-date=January 7, 2022|website=Premiere Speakers Bureau}}</ref>

In 2005, Bates was inducted into the Greater Knoxville Sports Hall of Fame. He was also named to the 100 Year All Tennessee Team. In 2011, Bates was awarded the Tom Landry Legend Award.<ref name="premiere" />

'''William Glenn Brundige''' (November 13, 1948 – December 29, 2018) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[defensive end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Washington Redskins]] for eight seasons, from 1970 through 1977.  He is currently sixth on the Redskins all-time sack list.

Born in [[Holyoke, Colorado]], Brundige played [[high school football]] at tiny [[Haxtun, Colorado|Haxtun]] in northeastern Colorado and then played [[college football]] at the [[University of Colorado]] in [[Boulder, Colorado|Boulder]]. He was a physics major at CU and also threw the [[shot put]] for the [[Colorado Buffaloes track and field]] team.<ref name=tuscnphy>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=ZhkfAAAAIBAJ&sjid=C5wEAAAAIBAJ&pg=3441%2C1757271 |newspaper=Tuscaloosa News |location=Alabama |title=Big step for a big Buff: doghouse to All-America |date=December 9, 1969 |page=11 }}</ref> After a senior season in 1969 in which he was named first-team [[1969 College Football All-America Team|All-America]], he was selected in the second round of the [[1970 NFL draft]], 43rd overall, by head coach [[Vince Lombardi]] of the Redskins.<ref name=wftgb>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=nMtNAAAAIBAJ&sjid=NooDAAAAIBAJ&pg=4290%2C2901058 |newspaper=Free Lance-Star |location=Fredericksburg, Virginia |title=Washington fortunate to get Brundige – Vince |date=January 28, 1970 |page=10 }}</ref><ref name=bblrel>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=eetNAAAAIBAJ&sjid=h4oDAAAAIBAJ&pg=7129%2C4723735 |newspaper=Free Lance-Star |location=Fredericksburg, Virginia |last=Buttram |first=Bill |title=Big Bill looks real |date=August 14, 1970 |page=6 }}</ref>

At age 21, he was a starter as a rookie in 1970 at defensive tackle. At the end of his third season in the NFL, Brundige became a part of both Redskin and Super Bowl lore in [[Super Bowl VII]]. He blocked the field goal attempt by [[Garo Yepremian]] that led to the bizarre fumble-return touchdown by [[Mike Bass]] that cut the [[1972 Miami Dolphins season|Miami Dolphins]]' lead to 14–7 with just over two minutes remaining.<ref name=dpfpw>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=uQZIAAAAIBAJ&sjid=EoEMAAAAIBAJ&pg=7036%2C2115334 |newspaper=Victoria Advocate |location=Texas |agency=(Los Angeles Times) |last=Solomon |first=George |title=Dolphins find perfect way to end season |date=January 15, 1973 |page=1B}}</ref><ref name=watnw>{{cite news |url=http://www.hailmagazine.com/archives/1045 |publisher=Hail! |last=Gehman |first=Jim |title=Where are they now - Bill Brundige |access-date=February 12, 2016}}</ref>

In [[2002 Washington Redskins season|2002]] for the Redskins' 70th anniversary, Brundige was named a member of the [[Washington Redskins#90 Greatest|70 Greatest Redskins]].

After his playing days, Brundige was a general manager of [[Ford Motor Company|Ford]] dealerships in the [[Shenandoah Valley]] region of [[Virginia]] in the city of  [[Winchester, Virginia|Winchester]] and town of [[Front Royal, Virginia|Front Royal]].<ref name=watnw/>

Brundige died at his home in [[Knoxville, Tennessee]] on December 29, 2018, from cancer.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.denverpost.com/2019/01/03/colorado-buffaloes-bill-brundige-washington-redskins-super-bowl-nfl/|title = CU football giant Bill Brundige passes away at age 70|date = 4 January 2019}}</ref>
