Defensive backs coach | highlights = ; As a player * 2× First-team [[All-Pro]] ([[1971 All-Pro Team|1971]], [[1972 All-Pro Team|1972]]) * 3× [[Pro Bowl]] ([[1972 Pro Bowl|1971]]–[[1974 Pro Bowl|1973]]) * 2× [[List of NFL annual interceptions leaders|NFL interceptions Leader]] (1971, 1972) * [[Philadelphia Eagles Hall of Fame]] ; As a coach * 2× [[List of Grey Cup champions|Grey Cup champion]] ([[84th Grey Cup|1996]], [[85th Grey Cup|1997]]) | statlabel1 = Games played | statvalue1 = 114 | statlabel2 = [[Starting lineup|Starts]] | statvalue2 = 80 | statlabel3 = [[Interception]]s | statvalue3 = 34 | statlabel4 = [[Fumble|Fumble recoveries]] | statvalue4 = 9 | statlabel5 = [[Punt (gridiron football)|Punts]] | statvalue5 = 213 | statlabel6 = Punting yards | statvalue6 = 8,316 (39.0 average) | statlabel7 = [[Return yards]] | statvalue7 = 1,517 | statlabel8 = Touchdowns | statvalue8 = 1 | pfr = BradBi00 }} '''William Calvin Bradley''' (born January 24, 1947) is an American former [[Gridiron football|football]] player and coach. He played professionally as a [[Safety (gridiron football position)|safety]], [[Punter (gridiron football)|punter]] and [[return specialist]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), earning [[All-Pro]] honors twice. He played with the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] for most of his career. As an assistant coach he won two [[Grey Cup]]s in the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL). He was also the defensive backs coach of the [[San Antonio Commanders]] of the [[Alliance of American Football]]. ==Early life== A native of [[Palestine, Texas]], Bradley was a [[quarterback]] at [[Palestine Independent School District|Palestine High School]]. With Bradley as quarterback, Palestine won the 1964 Texas 3A State Championship, the only one in the school's history. His running and passing skills gained him selection as a high school [[All-America]]n. His football talents, including the reputed ability to pass with either hand, earned him the nickname "Super Bill."{{cite news |last=Partsch III |first=Raymond A. |date=April 16, 2014 |title=Like a movie: Bill Bradley's life reads like a screenplay |url=http://www.beaumontenterprise.com/sports/lamar/article/Like-a-movie-Bill-Bradley-s-life-reads-like-a-5405356.php |newspaper=Beaumont Enterprise |location=Beaumont | access-date=May 9, 2014 }} He also participated in the Big 33 football game for the Texas All-Stars in 1966. His father was a baseball coach and Bradley dreamed of playing professional baseball. He was a talented shortstop who was selected by the Detroit Tigers in the 7th Round of the 1965 Major League Baseball draft. He was offered $20,000 to sign, but turned it down because he wanted to go to college. Instead, he played semi-pro ball with the Palestine Pals. ==College career== Bradley entered the [[University of Texas at Austin]] in 1965 and became the [[Starting lineup|starting]] quarterback and punter in 1966 as a sophomore. In 1966, he led the Longhorns to a 7–4 record and a victory over Mississippi in the Bluebonnet Bowl. Injured during a win over [[Indiana University|Indiana]], he sat out the Oklahoma game in favor of back-up Andy White, and [[University of Oklahoma|Oklahoma]] notched its first win in the rivalry since 1957. Bradley came back the following week and finished the season as the [[Southwest Conference]]'s leader for rushing touchdowns with 6. In the Bluebonnet Bowl, Bradley and running back [[Chris Gilbert (American football)|Chris Gilbert]] each ran for over 100 yards, marking the first time that two Longhorns had run for over 100 yards in the same bowl game. Bradley was starting quarterback again the next season. Texas started the season ranked #5, but back-to-back losses to #4 USC and Texas Tech knocked them from the rankings. They then ran off 6 straight wins before ending the season with another pair of back-to-back losses, this time to TCU and Texas A&M to finish 6-4 and missing out on a bowl game. Despite the down year, Bradley led the Southwest Conference in total touchdowns with 14. In 1968, Texas started the season ranked #5 and introduced the [[wishbone formation]] on offense, with co-captain Bradley at quarterback. Struggling with the new offense, Texas with Bradley under center tied #11 Houston and lost to Texas Tech. [[James Street (quarterback)|James Street]] replaced Bradley during the 3rd quarter of the Texas Tech game and never relinquished the position, leading the Longhorns to 9 consecutive wins, a Southwest Conference Championship and victory in the Cotton Bowl. Bradley was moved to [[wide receiver]] for two weeks, and then to defensive back and kick-off returner. As a defensive back he set the Texas and Southwest Conference records for most interceptions in a game when he picked off [[Texas A&M Aggies football|Texas A&M]] four times at the end of the regular season. His final game as a Longhorn was the 36–13 win over Tennessee in the Cotton Bowl. He then played in the 1969 [[Hula Bowl]], the Coaches All-America Game and the [[College All-Star Game]].{{cite web|url=http://www.lamarcardinals.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/bill_bradley_799507.html |title=Bill Bradley |website=LamarCardinals.com |access-date=September 3, 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140904112950/http://www.lamarcardinals.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/bill_bradley_799507.html |archive-date= September 4, 2014 }} ===Records=== * UT – Most passing yards, game (220 yards), broke his own record set earlier that year, surpassed by [[Rick McIvor]] in 1979 * '''UT – Longest punt, bowl game (74 yards)''' * UT – Most Offensive Yards, season (1,624),{{cite web|url=http://archives.starkcenter.org/bitstream/handle/11048/27670/LowryAlan.pdf?sequence=1 |title=Archive of Alan Lowry reports and clippings |website=.starkcenter.org |access-date=May 27, 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140528013257/http://archives.starkcenter.org/bitstream/handle/11048/27670/LowryAlan.pdf?sequence=1 |archive-date=May 28, 2014 }} surpassed by [[Earl Campbell]] in 1977 * '''Southwest Conference and UT – Most interceptions caught, game (4)''' Bold means still active ==NFL career== Bradley was selected in the third round of the [[1969 NFL/AFL draft]] by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] as a punter/defensive back. His first season he [[Punter (football position)|punted]] and returned [[kick returner|kick-offs]] and [[punt returner|punts]]. The next season, he was just the punter. In 1971, he finally moved to defense, became the back-up punter and was a returner again. It was on defense that he stood out. He went on to earn three [[All-Pro]] selections (1971–73) at [[Safety (American football position)|free safety]], including first-team All-Pro in 1971 and 1972. He also played in three [[Pro Bowl]]s from 1971 to 1973. His last full season of punting was 1972. He continued returning kick-offs and punts off and on for the rest of his career. Bradley led the NFL in interceptions in both 1971 (11) and 1972 (9), the first player ever to lead the league in interceptions in consecutive seasons, a feat matched only once since. In 1971, he also led the NFL in yards after an interception with 248. These achievements did not draw widespread attention, though, as the Eagles' record for those 2 years was 6–7–1 and 2–11–1; and the Eagles never made the playoffs during Bradley's tenure. He played his final year as the Eagle free safety in 1976, replaced by [[Deac Sanders|John Sanders]]. Bradley would later recount that during his years with the Eagles, he would spend nights out on dates with members of the [[hot pants patrol|Philadelphia Phillies usherettes]].{{cite news|last=Partsch III|first=Raymond A.|date=April 16, 2014|title=Like a movie: Bill Bradley's life reads like a screenplay|url=https://www.beaumontenterprise.com/sports/lamar/article/Like-a-movie-Bill-Bradley-s-life-reads-like-a-5405356.php|work=Beautmont Enterprise|location=Beaumont, Texas|access-date=September 2, 2018|archive-date=October 15, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181015141658/https://www.beaumontenterprise.com/sports/lamar/article/Like-a-movie-Bill-Bradley-s-life-reads-like-a-5405356.php|url-status=dead}} In 1977, Philadelphia traded Bradley to the Minnesota Vikings for a 7th round draft pick, but the Vikings cut him in training camp in favor of [[Paul Krause]]. Bradley went into retirement, working in his family's restaurant in Palestine, but in November of that year he was signed by the [[History of the St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]] when [[Mike Sensibaugh]] broke his leg. He had been asked to come back by other teams – including Houston, Oakland and Pittsburgh,{{cite news |last=Glenn |first=Sheeley |date=November 16, 1977 |title=Bradley back in time to renew feud? |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1144&dat=19771116&id=czYcAAAAIBAJ&sjid=OloEAAAAIBAJ&pg=7017,759057 |newspaper=The Pittsburgh Press |access-date=May 9, 2014 }} but only accepted with St. Louis because they looked to be playoff-bound. But they lost all their remaining games that season and stayed home. Bradley played four games as a defensive back with the Cardinals and then retired for good.{{cite news |date=November 29, 1977 |title=Timing Right for Bradley |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1955&dat=19771129&id=zN8hAAAAIBAJ&sjid=EaEFAAAAIBAJ&pg=3355,5735142 |newspaper=Reading Eagle |location=Reading, Pennsylvania |access-date=May 9, 2014 }} Bradley is a member of the Texas High School, University of Texas, Philadelphia Eagles and Texas Sports Halls of Fame. ===Records=== * Eagles – Interceptions, season (11) * Eagles – Interceptions, career (34), tied by [[Brian Dawkins]] and [[Eric Allen]] * Eagles – Interception return yards, season (249) * Eagles – Interception return yards, career (536) ==Coaching career== After retiring from the NFL, Bradley worked an assortment of jobs. He had invested in a sports management company based in Philadelphia, but sold his shares in 1980 and went back to Palestine where he bought a farm and ran a gas station he owned. He also worked as a host on Norwegian Cruise lines in the 1980s and '90s. Bradley's first coaching assignment was as defensive backs coach for the [[San Antonio Gunslingers (USFL team)|San Antonio Gunslingers]] of the fledgling [[United States Football League|USFL]] in 1983–1984. From there he moved on to the [[Memphis Showboats]] with [[head coach]] [[Pepper Rodgers]] in 1985. When the USFL folded, Bradley went back to The University of Texas as a voluntary assistant coach in 1987 for new head coach [[David McWilliams (American football)|David McWilliams]]. He was then hired by head coach [[Wally Buono]] as the defensive back coach and defensive coordinator for the [[Calgary Stampeders]] of the [[Canadian Football League]] from 1988 to 1990. Coach [[Mike Riley (American football)|Mike Riley]] asked Bradley to coach the secondary for him in the [[World League of American Football]] (WLAF) as his defensive back coach from 1991 to 1993. Bradley then went back to the CFL and coached with [[Kay Stephenson]] for the [[San Antonio Texans|Sacramento Gold Miners/San Antonio Texans]] in 1994–1995 as defensive coordinator before moving back to Canada with the [[Toronto Argonauts]]. There he helped win two [[Grey Cup]]s in 1996 and 1997. Success in Canada gave Bradley his first chance to coach in the NFL. From 1998 to 2000, he served as defensive backs coach for [[Wade Phillips]], [[Ted Cottrell]] and the [[Buffalo Bills]] before moving to the same position with the [[New York Jets]] from 2001 to 2003. Bradley returned to college coaching when his former Eagle teammate [[Guy Morriss]] hired him to be defensive coordinator for 2004–2006 at [[Baylor University]]. He then returned to the NFL to reunite with Defensive Coordinator Ted Cottrell as the [[San Diego Chargers]] secondary coach from 2006 to 2008. In early 2009, Bradley and three other assistants were fired.{{cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3831271 |title=Bradley, Barone among four fired | date=January 14, 2009 |website=ESPN.com |access-date=May 9, 2014}} During 2009 and 2010, he was the secondary coach for the [[Florida Tuskers]] of the [[United Football League (2009)|United Football League]].{{cite news |title=United Football League Announces Coaching Staffs For Its Franchises |url=http://ufl-football.com/press/2009/05/19/united_football_league_announces_coaching_staffs_for_its_franchises |work=UFL-football.com |date=May 19, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090626210310/http://www.ufl-football.com/press/2009/05/19/united_football_league_announces_coaching_staffs_for_its_franchises |archive-date=June 26, 2009 }} Bradley was hired to be the secondary coach of the Hartford Colonials in the UFL but the league pulled the plug on the team for lack of funds before he could coach a game. In 2012, Bradley was hired by [[Ray Woodard]] as the defensive coordinator of the [[Lamar Cardinals football]] team.{{cite web|url=http://www.lamarcardinals.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/030512aaa.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120907234710/http://www.lamarcardinals.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/030512aaa.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=September 7, 2012 |date=March 5, 2012 |title=Woodard adds three football assistants }} He retired from Lamar, and from coaching, in 2014, in part to help take care of his stepson who had suffered brain trauma as the result of a violent attack. In 2019, Bradley was the defensive backs coach of the [[San Antonio Commanders]] of the AAF until the league went bankrupt.{{cite web |last1=Alper |first1=Josh |title=AAF teams continue building coaching staffs |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/aaf-teams-continue-building-coaching-175926933.html |website=Yahoo Sports |access-date=November 1, 2018 |archive-date=October 10, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181010134659/https://sports.yahoo.com/aaf-teams-continue-building-coaching-175926933.html |url-status=dead }} He came out of retirement to serve as '''Bernard Karmell Pollard''' (born December 23, 1984) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Safety (American football position)|safety]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Purdue Boilermakers football|Purdue Boilermakers]], and was selected by the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in the second round of the [[2006 NFL draft]]. He has also played for the [[Houston Texans]], [[Baltimore Ravens]] and [[Tennessee Titans]]. Pollard was dubbed "'''the Bonecrusher'''" while at Purdue for his hard hits and [[Tackle (football move)|tackles]], and acquired the nickname "'''Patriot-Killer'''" as a professional, after inflicting injuries which would ultimately alter four [[New England Patriots]] seasons,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://kan.scout.com/2/663841.html |title=Pollard Bio |access-date=2009-01-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090523130010/http://kan.scout.com/2/663841.html |archive-date=2009-05-23 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=http://nesn.com/2012/01/bernard-pollard-fine-with-patriots-killer-reputation-hopes-giants-put-a-thrashing-on-new-england-in/|title=Bernard Pollard 'Fine' With Patriots-Killer Reputation, Hopes Giants 'Put a Thrashing' on New England in Super Bowl|date=2012-01-25|newspaper=NESN.com|language=en-US|access-date=2017-01-20}}</ref> including ending Patriots [[quarterback]] [[Tom Brady]]'s [[2008 New England Patriots season|2008 season]].

==Early life==
Pollard attended [[South Side High School (Fort Wayne, Indiana)|South Side High School]] in [[Fort Wayne, Indiana]], and was a [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] in [[High school football|football]], [[basketball]] and [[Track and field|track & field]]. In football, as a senior, he was selected as ''[[The News-Sentinel]]'' Area Player of the Year, and was a first-team All-State honoree. In track, he competed in the [[long jump]] (PR of 6.60m) and as a member of the [[4 x 100 metres relay|4 × 100 m]] (42.83s) relay squad.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.trackingfootball.com/players/bernard-pollard-1086/ |title=Bernard Pollard | Purdue | Chiefs DB |access-date=2014-10-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141023184959/https://www.trackingfootball.com/players/bernard-pollard-1086/ |archive-date=2014-10-23 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==College career==
Pollard played three years at [[Purdue University]]. As a Freshman, he was named a First-team Freshman [[All-American]] by [[College Football News|Collegefootballnews.com]], a second-team by ''[[The Sporting News]]'' and was selected to the [[Big Ten]] All-Freshman team by ''The Sporting News'' in 2003. He compiled 66 tackles (42 solo), one [[Pass deflected|pass break-up]] and one [[fumble]] recovery.

In 2004, he was named as a second-team All-Big Ten by coaches and honorable mention by the media. He led the team with 96 tackles (58 solo), 2 forced fumbles, 1 [[Quarterback sack|sack]], five pass break-ups and one [[interception]] He also blocked four kicks (two [[Punt (gridiron football)|punts]], one [[extra point]] and one [[Field goal (football)|field goal]]).

Pollard's final year at Purdue was marred by altercations with coaches, the height of which occurred in the beginning of the season when he asked [[head coach]] [[Joe Tiller]] to "Give me my papers", indicating the preference to transfer.  Tiller did not grant the transfer request, but the incident proved a precursor to a tumultuous final year. Despite this Pollard still compiled 92 tackles (64 solo), 3 interceptions, 3 pass break-ups, 1 fumble recovery and 1 blocked punt. His 5 blocked punts are a Purdue record.

===Kansas City Chiefs===
[[File:Bernard Pollard.JPG|thumb|left|250px|Pollard practicing with the Chiefs in 2007]]
Pollard was selected in the second round, 54th overall of the 2006 NFL Draft by the [[Kansas City Chiefs]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2006 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2006/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-09 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Pollard played the majority of his [[rookie]] season on [[special teams]] and ended the year with 10 tackles, 1 pass break-up, 1 forced fumble and 3 blocked punts, one against [[Arizona Cardinals|Arizona]], one against [[San Diego Chargers|San Diego]], and one against [[Jacksonville Jaguars|Jacksonville]] (recovered in the [[end zone]] for a touchdown). Pollard was a [[Starting lineup|starter]] in the [[2007 NFL season]]. Those three blocked punts rank second in Chiefs history, trailing only Chiefs Hall of Fame CB [[Albert Lewis (American football)|Albert Lewis]] (1983–1993) who recorded 10.<ref name="Kansas City Chiefs bio">[http://www.kcchiefs.com/player/bernard_pollard/ Kansas City Chiefs bio] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080627113719/http://www.kcchiefs.com/player/bernard_pollard/ |date=June 27, 2008 }}</ref>

Pollard's blocked punt against the Jacksonville Jaguars, he blocked a [[Chris Hanson (American football)|Chris Hanson]] punt and recovered for a touchdown, he helped propel the Kansas City Chiefs to a 35–30 win and an eventual playoff berth. He earned AFC Special Teams Player of the Week honors.<ref name="Kansas City Chiefs bio" />

He also blocked a punt against the [[Denver Broncos]], in [[2007 Kansas City Chiefs season#Week 10: vs. Denver Broncos|week ten of the 2007 season]], that went out of the end zone for a [[Safety (American football score)|safety]]. The Chiefs eventually lost, 27 to 11. In the [[2007 Kansas City Chiefs season|2007 season]], he intercepted his first NFL pass off [[Carson Palmer]] against the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] on October 14. Pollard also intercepted [[Jon Kitna]] in the game against [[Detroit Lions]] on December 23.<ref name="Kansas City Chiefs bio" />

On September 7, 2008, Pollard was involved in a play that ended with [[New England Patriots]] quarterback [[Tom Brady]] being taken off the field with a knee injury and not returning for the rest of the game. It was later revealed that Pollard's hit on Brady had ended the quarterback's season.<ref name="Injury to Tom Brady deals Super quest fatal blow">{{cite web|url=http://news.bostonherald.com/sports/football/patriots/view/2008_09_07_Injury_to_Tom_Brady_deals_Super_quest_fatal_blow/srvc=home&position=also|title=Injury to Tom Brady deals Super quest fatal blow|last=Tomase|first=John|date=2008-09-08|publisher=The Boston Herald|access-date=2008-09-08|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080910210900/http://news.bostonherald.com/sports/football/patriots/view/2008_09_07_Injury_to_Tom_Brady_deals_Super_quest_fatal_blow/srvc%3Dhome%26position%3Dalso|archive-date=2008-09-10}}</ref> Pollard later apologized for the hit, saying, "It was really an accident, I can't change what happened. I can't do anything but pray for him and hope he has a speedy recovery."  The Brady hit, along with other cases where quarterbacks had suffered serious injuries on similar helmet-to-knee hits, resulted in a rules change in the NFL beginning with the 2009 season: a defensive player on the ground may no longer lunge or dive at the quarterback's lower legs.<ref name="NFL Continues re-writing the rule book">{{cite web|url=https://sports.yahoo.com/nfl/blog/shutdown_corner/post/The-NFL-continues-the-re-writing-of-the-rule-boo?urn=nfl,150662|title=The NFL Continues the Re-Writing of the rule book|last=D|first=MJ|date=2009-03-26|publisher=Yahoo|access-date=2009-03-26}}</ref>

Pollard was Kansas City's leading tackler with a career-high 98 tackles in 2008 (84 solo) with one for loss, an interception, four passes defensed, two forced fumbles and three fumble recoveries.<ref name="Kansas City Chiefs bio" />

On September 5, 2009, the Chiefs released Pollard.<ref name="final cuts">{{cite web|title=Chiefs announce roster moves |url=http://kcchiefs.com/news/2009/09/05/chiefs_announce_roster_moves/ |publisher=Kansas City Chiefs |date=2009-09-05 |access-date=2009-09-05 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090908145739/http://www.kcchiefs.com/news/2009/09/05/chiefs_announce_roster_moves |archive-date=September 8, 2009 }}</ref>

===Houston Texans===
Pollard signed with the [[Houston Texans]] on September 24, 2009. In his first year with Houston, Pollard had a career year, racking up 102 tackles (81 solo), 1.5 sacks, 4 interceptions, as well as two defensive touchdowns. He had 111 tackles and four forced fumbles the next year.

===Baltimore Ravens===
[[File:Cary Williams, Ed Reed, Bernard Pollard.JPG|thumb|right|250px|[[Cary Williams]] (29), [[Ed Reed]] (20) and Pollard (31) at [[Navy–Marine Corps Memorial Stadium]] in August 2012]]
On August 3, 2011, Pollard signed a two-year deal with the [[Baltimore Ravens]], replacing [[Dawan Landry]], who had departed in free agency. While playing on the Ravens defense in 2011, Pollard recorded 75 tackles, two sacks, three forced fumbles, and an interception. On May 8, 2012, the Ravens signed Pollard to a three-year contract extension.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ravens give S Pollard three-year extension|url=http://www.cbssports.com/nfl/rapid-reports/post/18993943|work=CBS Sports}}</ref> On October 26, Pollard was fined $7,875 for an unnecessary roughness penalty in Week 7 against the [[Houston Texans]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nfl.com/news/fines-roundup-alphonso-smith-docked-for-horse-collar-tackle-0ap1000000085905|title=Fines roundup: Alphonso Smith docked for horse-collar tackle|work=[[National Football League]]|date=2012-10-26|access-date=2012-10-26}}</ref>

Pollard proved to be more effective and successful for the [[2012 Baltimore Ravens season|following season]], recording 98 tackles, two sacks and an interception in 13 starts.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/team/stats/_/name/bal/year/2012|work=ESPN.com|access-date=2013-03-04|title=2012 Baltimore Ravens season}}</ref> Despite missing the last three weeks due to a chest injury sustained against the [[Washington Redskins]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.baltimoreravens.com/news/article-1/Terrell-Suggs-Active-Bernard-Pollard-Out-vs-Broncos/b53c5bd7-b59f-4cd6-a96e-b5035edab381|title=Terrell Suggs Active, Bernard Pollard Out vs. Broncos|work=BaltimoreRavens.com|date=2012-12-16|access-date=2013-03-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130927171507/http://www.baltimoreravens.com/news/article-1/Terrell-Suggs-Active-Bernard-Pollard-Out-vs-Broncos/b53c5bd7-b59f-4cd6-a96e-b5035edab381|archive-date=2013-09-27|url-status=dead}}</ref> Pollard ended the regular season as the team's leading tackler. He would return for [[2012–13 NFL playoffs|the postseason]], forcing a key fumble against the [[New England Patriots]] in the AFC Championship game and then winning his first [[Super Bowl XLVII|Super Bowl]] ring with the team.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/201302030sfo.htm |title=Super Bowl XLVII - San Francisco 49ers vs. Baltimore Ravens - February 3rd, 2013 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en |access-date=2017-11-08}}</ref> He revealed after the season that he had been playing with a rib injury for nearly the entire season, as he sustained the injury during the Week 2 meeting against the [[Philadelphia Eagles]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2013/02/04/bernard-pollard-played-with-six-cracked-ribs/|title=Bernard Pollard played with six cracked ribs|work=[[Pro Football Talk]]|date=2013-02-14|access-date=2013-03-04}}</ref>

In an interview with [[CBSSports.com]]'s Clark Judge, Pollard claimed that unless significant changes are made, the NFL will cease to exist in 30 years.  He said that while the league was making great strides toward making the game safer, players were becoming so big and so strong that concussions and other serious injuries would still continue to escalate.  Eventually, Pollard said, "there's going to come a point where fans are going to get fed up with it" and stop watching.<ref>Judge, Clark. [http://www.cbssports.com/nfl/blog/clark-judge/21613854/ravens-pollard-nfl-really-does-stand-for-not-for-long Ravens' Pollard: NFL really does stand for Not For Long]. [[CBSSports.com]], 2013-01-28.</ref>
On March 13, 2013, Pollard was released by the Ravens.<ref>{{cite tweet|user=Crushboy31|author=Bernard Pollard Jr|number=311844036031946753|date=13 March 2013|title=Well Raven Nation it's been fun. My time in Baltimore is done... Thank you!}}</ref>

===Tennessee Titans===
[[File:LaRod Stephens-Howling.jpg|thumb|left|250px|Pollard tackling [[Pittsburgh Steelers|Steelers]] [[running back]] [[LaRod Stephens-Howling]] in 2013.]] 
On March 21, 2013, Pollard signed a one-year deal with the [[Tennessee Titans]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sbnation.com/nfl/2013/3/21/4131598/bernard-pollard-signs-tennessee-titans|title=Bernard Pollard, Titans agree on 1-year contract|date=2013-03-21|last=Titans|first=Pollard|publisher=SBNATION|access-date=2013-03-21}}</ref> On August 17, 2013, Pollard was fined $10,000 for a late hit on Aldrick Robinson during Preseason Week 2 against the Washington Redskins. On September 18, 2013, Pollard was fined $42,000 for a hit on Andre Johnson that led to Johnson getting a concussion. In 16 games of the 2013 year, Pollard made 99 combined tackles with 0.5 sacks, 3 interceptions, and 5 passes defended.

On March 3, 2014, Pollard and the Titans had agreed on a new two-year contract, keeping him in Tennessee through the [[2015 NFL season]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Wesseling|first=Chris|title=Bernard Pollard agrees to terms with Tennessee Titans|url=https://www.nfl.com/news/bernard-pollard-tennessee-titans-strike-contract-0ap2000000330431|work=NFL.com|access-date=3 March 2014}}</ref> During Week 5 against the [[Cleveland Browns]], Pollard suffered an Achilles tendon injury following a Browns' go-ahead touchdown. The next day, an MRI revealed that his Achilles tendon was considered ruptured, prematurely ending his 2014 season. In 5 games, Pollard made 27 tackles with a sack and a pass defended. He was officially placed on injured reserve on October 8.<ref>{{cite news|work=NBCSports.com|url=http://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2014/10/08/titans-place-bernard-pollard-on-ir-sign-brandon-ghee/|title=Titans place Bernard Pollard on IR, sign Brandon Ghee|first=Josh|last=Alper|date=October 8, 2014|access-date=2014-10-20}}</ref>

In the early off-season, Pollard requested a release. On March 3, 2015, Pollard was released by the Titans.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2015/07/30/bernard-pollard-says-hes-healthy-and-ready-to-play/ | title=Bernard Pollard says he's healthy and ready to play | date=30 July 2015 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|work=NFL.com|url=https://www.nfl.com/news/tennessee-titans-release-safety-bernard-pollard-0ap3000000475926|title=Titans to release safety Bernard Pollard|date=March 2, 2015|access-date=2015-03-02}}</ref>

==="The Patriot Killer"===
{{multiple image
| align        = right
| total_width  = 550
| image1       = Tom Brady 2017.JPG
| image2       = Wes Welker at Patriots at Raiders 12-14-08 3.JPG
| image3       = Rob Gronkowski.JPG
| image4       = Stevan Ridley.JPG
| footer       = In four different seasons, [[New England Patriots]] players (L to R) [[Tom Brady]], [[Wes Welker]], [[Rob Gronkowski]], and [[Stevan Ridley]] all suffered injuries of varying degrees by Pollard, significantly altering the Patriots' postseason chances.
}}
Beginning in 2008, while Pollard was with the Kansas City Chiefs, a series of events began to take place that would alter the course of four Patriots' seasons.

During the first week of the 2008 season, Pollard was knocked to the ground while trying to sack Tom Brady. On the ground, Pollard lunged at Brady's legs, connecting his helmet to Brady's left knee and tearing the quarterback's anterior cruciate and medial collateral ligaments. Brady's season was prematurely over, and the season marked only the second time (the other being [[2002 New England Patriots season|2002]]) in the [[Brady–Belichick era]] where the team missed the playoffs.<ref name="washingtontimes.com">{{Cite web |last=Butt |first=Jason |date=September 19, 2012 |title=Bernard Pollard vs. Pats: Seek and destroy |url=http://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2012/sep/19/bernard-pollard-vs-pats-seek-and-destroy/?page=all |access-date=2025-07-19 |website=[[The Washington Times]]}}</ref>

In 2009, while Pollard was with the Houston Texans, Brady threw a pass to [[Wes Welker]] to the short left side of the field, which he then took up the field. Pollard closed in on Welker fast, forcing the diminutive receiver to cut to his right, possibly faster than he anticipated. His left plant foot slipped and he tore his ACL and MCL, missing the playoffs that year.<ref name="washingtontimes.com" />

In the AFC Championship Game following the 2011 season, Patriots tight end [[Rob Gronkowski]] caught a pass of about 20 yards with Pollard in coverage. Pollard, now a member of the Baltimore Ravens, wrapped Gronkowski up to take him to the ground. As Gronkowski hit the turf, Pollard's right thigh forcefully landed on Gronkowski's left ankle. Gronkowski suffered a high ankle sprain. Gronkowski played in the Super Bowl two weeks later, but the injury limited him to just two catches for 26 yards.<ref name="washingtontimes.com" />

In the fourth quarter of the 2012 AFC Championship Game, as the Patriots were driving in an attempt to tie the game, Pollard launched a direct helmet-to-helmet hit which concussed running back [[Stevan Ridley]]. Ridley immediately lost consciousness and control of the ball, which was scooped up by the Ravens to take over possession, while wide receiver [[Brandon Lloyd]] tended to his fallen teammate. This sealed the Ravens' victory, advancing them to Super Bowl XLVII, in which they defeated the San Francisco 49ers. Though Ridley recovered in time to play in the 2013 NFL season, he was unable to retain his job as a starter, and was released by five different NFL teams since 2013.

Pollard was also the final player to tackle Aaron Hernandez in an NFL game.

'''Bernardo Harris''' (born October 15, 1971) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]]. He attended Chapel Hill High School, graduating in 1990. He was recruited by [[Mack Brown]] to play [[college football]] for the [[North Carolina Tar Heels football]]. After not being drafted, he was signed as a free agent by the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in 1994. At Kansas City, Harris injured his knee in the first week of training camp and was out of football.<ref>{{cite web |last=Hendricks |first=Martin |url=http://www.jsonline.com/sports/packers/29385949.html |title=Taking nothing for granted |publisher=Jsonline.com |date=2007-11-29 |accessdate=2014-04-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120625223834/http://www.jsonline.com/sports/packers/29385949.html |archive-date=2012-06-25 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Bernardo Harris became a free agent and was signed by the [[Green Bay Packers]] in 1995, playing in eleven games his rookie season. Harris played for the Packers for seven seasons<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/H/HarrBe20.htm |title=Bernardo Harris NFL Football Statistics |publisher=Pro-Football-Reference.com |date=1971-10-15 |accessdate=2014-04-17}}</ref> and played on the 1996 [[Super Bowl XXXI]] and 1997 [[Super Bowl XXXII]] teams.

In 2002, Harris was signed as a free agent by the Baltimore Ravens, after a shoulder injury to Ray Lewis. In 2003, Bernardo Harris was placed on the injured reserved and subsequently retired.

'''Bert Tyrone Emanuel''' (born October 26, 1970) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Atlanta Falcons]] in the second round of the [[1994 NFL draft]], 45th overall and the Falcons' first pick in the draft.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1994 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1994/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He also played for the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], [[Miami Dolphins]], [[New England Patriots]], and [[Detroit Lions]].

Emanuel played [[quarterback]] in [[college football|college]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bert Emanuel College Stats, School, Draft, Gamelog, Splits |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/bert-emanuel-1.html |access-date=2023-09-30 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He spent two seasons as a [[substitution (sport)|backup]] for the [[UCLA Bruins football|UCLA Bruins]] before transferring to the [[Rice Owls football|Rice Owls]] and [[starting lineup|starting]] at quarterback in his [[junior (education year)|junior]] and [[senior (education)|senior]] seasons.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Block |first=Randy |date=August 27, 1993 |title=Emanuel to Lead Football Team Against Top-25 Rivals |url=https://scholarship.rice.edu/bitstream/handle/1911/68121/thr19930827.pdf  |access-date=September 30, 2023 |website=Rice.edu}}</ref>

=="The Bert Emanuel Rule"==
While playing for the [[1999 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season|Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] against the [[1999 St. Louis Rams season|St. Louis Rams]] in the [[1999–2000 NFL playoffs#NFC Championship: St. Louis Rams 11, Tampa Bay Buccaneers 6|1999 NFC Championship Game]], Emanuel made a 13-yard reception at the Rams' 22 yard line with 47 seconds remaining in the game. The Buccaneers, trailing 11–6, called a quick timeout, and the reception would have given Tampa Bay a realistic chance to continue a potential game-winning drive. The ruling on the field initially was a complete pass. Despite the fact that Emanuel apparently controlled the ball at every point during the catch, booth replay official [[Jerry Markbreit]] ordered a review of the call. Referee [[Bill Carollo]] determined that the nose of the ball had touched the ground as he brought it into his body. The catch was overturned, and Tampa Bay went on to lose the game, 11–6.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.football.com/commentary/rossman/bucs_revenge.shtml |title=bucs revenge  |access-date=2009-09-15 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060525161731/http://www.football.com/commentary/rossman/bucs_revenge.shtml |archive-date=2006-05-25 }}</ref><ref>[http://www.bucpower.com/1899fennelly.html Bucpower.Com 1899 fennelly]</ref>

The ensuing controversy prompted the NFL to clarify the rule regarding what constitutes a valid pass reception. This would come to be known as "The Bert Emanuel Rule."<ref>{{cite news|url=http://si.cnn.com/football/nfl/news/2000/03/28/meetings_celebrations_ap/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120731052158/http://si.cnn.com/football/nfl/news/2000/03/28/meetings_celebrations_ap/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 31, 2012 |work=CNNSI.com |title=NFL competition committee advises reducing celebrations |date=March 28, 2000 }}</ref>

After retiring from football, Williams became a [[high school football]] coach and mentored his nephew, future NFL safety [[Eric Berry]]. Williams and his nephew opened a vintage car store and a juice bar.{{cite web | url=https://uga.rivals.com/news/catching-up-with-bernard-williams | title=UGASports - Catching up With… Bernard Williams | date=19 July 2019 | access-date=November 18, 2023 | archive-date=November 18, 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231118194601/https://uga.rivals.com/news/catching-up-with-bernard-williams | url-status=dead }} In 2015, after undergoing heart surgery, Williams stopped smoking marijuana. {{As of|2023}}, Williams was working toward a psychology degree, while working as a driver for [[Amazon (company)|Amazon]], volunteer firefighting, and restoring old cars.{{cite news |last=Bree |first=Matt |title=The Eagles released Bernard Williams 29 years after his final game. He found peace after flushing '$100 million down the drain.' |url=https://www.inquirer.com/eagles/eagles-waive-bernard-williams-nfl-suspended-marijuana-20231118.html |newspaper=The Philadelphia Inquirer |date=November 18, 2023 |access-date=November 19, 2023}} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *[https://web.archive.org/web/20070930153904/http://www.argonauts.ca/Argos/Team/Roster/Bernard_Williams.html Toronto Argonauts profile] (from [[Internet Archive]]) {{Navboxes|title=|list= {{EaglesFirstPick}} {{1994 NFL Draft}} {{Eagles1994DraftPicks}} {{92nd Grey Cup}} }} {{DEFAULTSORT:Williams, Bernard}} [[Category:1972 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:American football offensive tackles]] [[Category:BC Lions players]] [[Category:Canadian football offensive linemen]] [[Category:Detroit Fury players]] [[Category:Georgia Bulldogs football players]] [[Category:Memphis Maniax players]] [[Category:Philadelphia Eagles players]] [[Category:Toronto Argonauts players]] [[Category:Players of American football from Memphis, Tennessee]] [[Category:Players of Canadian football from Memphis, Tennessee]] [[Category:21st-century American sportsmen]] [[Category:21st-century African-American sportsmen]] [[Category:20th-century American sportsmen]] [[Category:20th-century African-American sportsmen]]

'''William T. Brooks Jr.''' (born April 6, 1964) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for 11 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). Brooks was selected by the [[Indianapolis Colts]] in the fourth round of the [[1986 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1986 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1986/draft.htm |access-date=October 2, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He played in the NFL from 1986 to 1996 for the Colts, [[Buffalo Bills]], and [[Washington Redskins]]. Brooks played [[college football]] for [[Boston University Terriers football|Boston University]].

==Early life==
Bill Brooks was born on April 6, 1964, in [[Boston, Massachusetts]] and raised in nearby [[Framingham, Massachusetts]]. Brooks attended [[Framingham High School|Framingham North High School]] where he was a two-sport star athlete in football and [[basketball]].<ref name="upper">{{cite web |last1=Boyle |first1=Michael |title=Bill Brooks: Upper Limit Success Story |url=http://office.biggerfasterstronger.com/uploads2/89_Feb_BillBrooks.pdf |website=Bigger Faster Stronger |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref>

On the football team, Brooks played both offense and defense. In 1980 as a junior, Brooks was named to the Bay State League All-Star team as a defensive back.<ref>{{cite news |title=The 1980 league all-star teams for Eastern Massachusetts |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe-the-1980-league-all-sta/146346795/ |access-date=April 30, 2024 |work=The Boston Globe |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |date=December 17, 1980}}</ref> In his senior season, Brooks continued to shine for Framingham. ''[[The Boston Globe]]'' named Brooks a Star of the Week in a 21-13 win over [[Braintree High School]]. Brooks had five receptions for 175 yards and two touchdowns and recorded four interceptions on defense.<ref>{{cite news |title=Stars of the week |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe-stars-of-the-week/146346982/ |access-date=April 30, 2024 |work=The Boston Globe |date=November 10, 1981}}</ref> Brooks was selected to play in the Massachusetts Shriners All-Star game, representing the South team. Brooks set a then-Shriners game record with 150 receiving yards and one touchdown.<ref>{{cite news |title=Fourth Shriners All-Star football game June 26 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe-fourth-shriners-all-sta/146346623/ |access-date=April 30, 2024 |work=The Boston Globe |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |date=April 6, 1982}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Gordon |first1=Ken |title=North Stuns South, 21-6 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe-north-stuns-south-21-6/146347097/ |access-date=April 30, 2024 |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |work=The Boston Globe |date=June 27, 1982}}</ref>

==College career==
Brooks played for [[Division I-AA]] Boston University (BU) from 1982 to 1985. Brooks saw varsity playing time as a freshman and in BU's first game of the season against [[New Hampshire Wildcats football|New Hampshire]], Brooks had two receptions for 23 yards and caught his first collegiate touchdown.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Eisenberg |first1=Harry |title=UNH comes alive, nips sluggish BU |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe-unh-comes-alive-nips-s/146347196/ |access-date=April 30, 2024 |work=The Boston Globe |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |date=September 19, 1982}}</ref> Brooks led BU with 30 receptions and placed second on the team in receiving yards. He was named the Yankee Conference Rookie of the Year and Second-Team All-Yankee Conference.<ref name="BUHOF">{{cite web |title=Bill Brooks |url=https://goterriers.com/honors/boston-university-athletic-hall-of-fame/bill-brooks/56 |website=Boston University Athletic Hall of Fame |publisher=Boston University Athletics |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref> That year, BU were [[1982 Boston University Terriers football team|Yankee Conference co-champions]] with [[Maine Black Bears football|Maine]] and faced [[Colgate Raiders football|Colgate]] in the first round of the [[1982 NCAA Division I-AA football season#Postseason|1982 NCAA Division I-AA Playoffs]], losing 21-7.

As a sophomore, Brooks and running back Paul Lewis led the Terriers to a 9-4 record and a tie for #13 in the Division I-AA rankings. BU repeated as [[1983 Boston University Terriers football team|Yankee Conference co-champions]], this time with [[Connecticut Huskies football|UConn]]. BU won their first round matchup in the [[1983 NCAA Division I-AA football season#Postseason|1983 NCAA Division I-AA Playoffs]], defeating [[Eastern Kentucky Colonels football|Eastern Kentucky]] 24-20. In the second round game against [[Furman Paladins football|Furman]], Brooks recorded 12 receptions for 234 yards, but BU lost to the #3-ranked Paladins, 35-16. Brooks was named to the All-Yankee Conference First-Team at the end of the season.<ref name=BUHOF /> Brooks set a new BU school record with 39 receptions on the season.<ref>{{cite news |last1=MacMullan |first1=Jackie |author-link=Jackie MacMullan |date=November 20, 1983 |title=BU humbles Morgan St. |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe-bu-humbles-morgan-st/146347756/ |access-date=April 30, 2024 |work=The Boston Globe |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>

In his junior season, Brooks again led the team in receiving while also becoming the first wide receiver to lead BU in scoring.<ref name=BUHOF /> BU played [[Grambling State Tigers football|Grambling State]] in the opening game of the season as part of the Whitney Young Memorial Classic at [[Yankee Stadium (1923)|Yankee Stadium]]. BU won the game 16-9 and Brooks recorded three receptions for 111 yards, including an 83-yard touchdown reception.<ref>{{cite news |last1=MacMullan |first1=Jackie |date=September 9, 1984 |title=BU wraps up Grambling early, 16-9 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe-bu-wraps-up-grambling-e/86092325/ |work=The Boston Globe |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> The Terriers went 9-3 and earned their third straight [[1984 Boston University Terriers football team|Yankee Conference co-championship]] with [[Rhode Island Rams football|Rhode Island]]. BU tied for the #4 ranking, and faced [[Richmond Spiders football|Richmond]] in the first round of the [[1984 NCAA Division I-AA football season#Postseason|1984 NCAA Division I-AA Playoffs]], where they lost 33-35. Brooks was named to the All-Yankee Conference First-Team and All-New England Intercollegiate First-Team.<ref name=BUHOF />

In Brooks' 1985 senior season, BU went 3-8 and missed the NCAA Division I-AA Playoffs for the first time in his career. Despite BU's poor record, Brooks had his most productive collegiate season. Brooks had 79 receptions for 1,210 yards and 11 touchdowns on the season. In his final collegiate game against Colgate, Brooks recorded 10 receptions for 236 yards and four touchdowns, setting a new BU single-game receiving touchdown record.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Monahan |first1=Bob |title=Bumbling BU loses its grip |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe-1985-colgate-bu/57226974/ |access-date=April 30, 2024 |work=The Boston Globe |date=November 24, 1985}}</ref> Brooks earned his third All-Yankee Conference First-Team selection, second All-New England First-Team selection, the 1985 ECAC Division I-AA First-Team, and AP All-America Second-Team.<ref>{{cite news |title=ECAC Div 1-AA Team |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe-ecac-div-1-aa-team/146350275/ |access-date=April 30, 2024 |work=The Boston Globe |via=[[Newspapers.com]]  |date=December 5, 1985}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=How NFL Scouts rate top New England prospects |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe-bill-brooks-wr-boston/146350493/ |access-date=April 30, 2024 |work=The Boston Globe |via=[[Newspapers.com]]  |date=April 27, 1986}}</ref> Brooks also played in the 1986 [[Senior Bowl]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Senior Bowl All-Time Roster |url=https://www.seniorbowl.com/the-game/all-time-roster/ |website=Reese's Senior Bowl |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref>

Brooks set several BU school records during his time in Boston, including most career receptions (228), career receiving yards (3,579), and career receiving touchdowns (32).<ref name=upper /> Brooks was named to the Boston University Athletic Hall of Fame in 1991.<ref name=BUHOF />

==Professional career==
Brooks was drafted by the [[Indianapolis Colts]] in the fourth round with the 86th overall selection in the [[1986 NFL draft]].<ref name="PFR">{{cite web |title=Bill Brooks |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BrooBi00.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref>

===Indianapolis Colts (1986–1992)===
Brooks had an immediate impact for the Colts during his rookie season. He recorded his first NFL touchdown reception in week four against the [[New York Jets]] on a three-yard pass from fellow rookie quarterback [[Jack Trudeau]].<ref>{{cite web |title=New York Jets at Indianapolis Colts - September 28th, 1986 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198609280clt.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref> The next week against the [[San Francisco 49ers]], Brooks recorded his longest career reception - an 84-yard touchdown from Trudeau.
<ref>{{cite web |title=Indianapolis Colts at San Francisco 49ers - October 5th, 1986 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198610050sfo.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref> In a week 11 rematch against the Jets, Brooks recorded his first 100-yard receiving game with nine catches for 177 yards and one touchdown.<ref>{{cite web |title=Indianapolis Colts at New York Jets - November 16th, 1986 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198611160nyj.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref> The following week against the [[Houston Oilers]], he turned in a seven catch, 105 yard performance that included two touchdowns.<ref>{{cite web |title=Indianapolis Colts at Houston Oilers - November 23rd, 1986 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198611230oti.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref> Brooks set Colts rookie records in all receiving categories, finishing the 1986 season with 65 receptions for 1,131 yards and eight touchdowns.<ref name=PFR /><ref name=JJ>{{cite web |last1=Stankevitz |first1=JJ |title=Black History Month: From his Ring of Honor career to current role, Bill Brooks is a Colts lifer |url=https://www.colts.com/news/black-history-month-from-his-ring-of-honor-career-to-current-role-bill-brooks-is-a-colts-lifer |website=Colts.com |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref> The Colts started the season at 0-13, firing head coach [[Rod Dowhower]] and replacing him with [[Ron Meyer]], who won the final three games of the season and brought the Colts to 3-13.<ref>{{cite web |title=1986 Indianapolis Colts Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/clt/1986.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref> Brooks was named to the [[PFWA All-Rookie Team#1986|1986 PFWA All-Rookie Team]].

In 1987, Brooks built on his rookie success. In week one against the [[Cincinnati Bengals]], Brooks had six receptions for 146 yards and one touchdown. His touchdown reception came on a 52-yard play where Brooks leapt over two defenders before running into the end zone.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Kitchell |first1=Dave |title=Trudeau has good outing, unfortunate last throw |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-kokomo-tribune-trudeau-has-good-outi/146355994/ |access-date=April 30, 2024 |work=The Kokomo Tribune |date=September 14, 1987}}</ref> Brooks finished the season with 51 receptions for 722 yards and three touchdowns. The Colts' play continued to improve under Meyer, with the addition of star running back [[Eric Dickerson]] providing a new offensive weapon. The Colts went 9-6 and won the [[AFC East]] Division during the [[1987 NFL season#The NFLPA strike|strike-shortened season]]. The Colts made their first NFL playoff appearance since moving to Indianapolis, losing in the Divisional Round 21-38 to the [[Cleveland Browns]].<ref>{{cite web |title=1987 Indianapolis Colts Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/clt/1987.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref>

The 1988 season saw a new quarterback for the Colts, with [[Chris Chandler (American football)|Chris Chandler]] being drafted in the third round. Chandler was thrust into the starting role as veteran [[Gary Hogeboom]] and Trudeau both suffered injuries. With Chandler at quarterback for the majority of the season, Brooks continued to show consistency. Brooks was injured in a preseason game against the [[Denver Broncos]], but was able to recover before the start of the regular season.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Bansch |first1=John |title=Colts sign Cribbs for duties as "H" backup |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-indianapolis-star-colts-sign-cribbs/146380393/ |access-date=April 30, 2024 |work=The Indianapolis Star |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |date=September 3, 1988}}</ref> Brooks had 54 receptions for 867 yards and three touchdowns on the season.<ref name=PFR /> Brooks' best game of the season came in week seven against the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]]. Brooks caught seven receptions for 139 yards and one touchdown, as the Colts held on to a 35-31 victory.<ref>{{cite web |title=Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Indianapolis Colts - October 16th, 1988 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198810160clt.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref> The Colts posted their second consecutive winning season, going 9-7 but finishing just outside of the playoffs at second place in the AFC East.<ref>{{cite web |title=1988 Indianapolis Colts Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/clt/1988.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref>

In 1989, Indianapolis drafted wide receiver [[Andre Rison]] in the first round. Coming into the season, Brooks held out of training camp in response to the much larger contract that the rookie Rison had received. Brooks negotiated a new three-year deal, and returned to the Colts in August.<ref>{{cite news |title=Brooks signs, Colts camp full |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1989/08/08/Brooks-signs-Colts-camp-full/1220618552000/ |access-date=April 30, 2024 |work=UPI Archives |agency=UPI |date=August 8, 1989}}</ref> Rison and Brooks both played well throughout the 1989 season, but poor quarterback play limited their effectiveness. Chris Chandler started the first three games of the season before suffering an ACL tear, leaving Trudeau to take the reins. For the season, Brooks recorded 63 catches for 919 yards and four touchdowns.<ref name=PFR /> Rison added 52 catches for 820 yards and four touchdowns. Brooks had three 100-yard receiving games on the season. The Colts went 8-8 on the season, missing the playoffs.<ref>{{cite web |title=1989 Indianapolis Colts Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/clt/1989.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref>

Brooks took over again in 1990 as the Colts premier pass catcher. Prior to the [[1990 NFL draft]], Indianapolis traded Rison and lineman [[Chris Hinton]] to the [[Atlanta Falcons]] for their first round selection. The Colts used that pick to take [[Jeff George]], who was seen as the new franchise quarterback. Brooks responded with another consistent season, recording 62 receptions for 823 yard and five touchdowns.<ref name=PFR /> The Colts went 7-9 on the season.<ref>{{cite web |title=1990 Indianapolis Colts Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/clt/1990.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref>

In 1991, the Colts started the season at 0-5, leading to head coach Ron Meyer being fired. Defensive coordinator [[Rick Venturi]] took over for the remainder of the season, but did not fare any better. The Colts won a single game on the season, finishing at 1-15.<ref>{{cite web |title=1991 Indianapolis Colts Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/clt/1991.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref> Brooks remained a consistent presence throughout the chaotic season. He made a career-high 72 catches for 888 yards and four touchdowns.<ref name=PFR />

The 1992 season was Brooks' last in Indianapolis as a player. He missed the opening game of the season with a sprained ankle, snapping a streak of 88 consecutive starts.<ref>{{cite news |title=Colts Notes |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-indianapolis-news-colts-notes/146383190/ |access-date=April 30, 2024 |work=The Indianapolis News |via=[[Newspapers.com]] |date=September 7, 1992}}</ref> Under new head coach [[Ted Marchibroda]], Brooks' playing time began to be limited. Receivers [[Jessie Hester]] and [[Reggie Langhorne]] took over as the primary pass catchers.<ref>{{cite news |title=Colts Notes |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-indianapolis-news-colts-notes/146383521/ |access-date=April 30, 2024 |work=The Indianapolis News |date=November 30, 1992}}</ref> Brooks still had a respectable season, and in 10 starts he recorded 44 receptions for 468 yards and one touchdown.<ref name=PFR />

Brooks' contract with the Colts expired after the 1992 season, leaving him a free agent. Several teams pursued him, including Indianapolis, but Brooks signed with the [[Buffalo Bills]] in April 1993.<ref>{{cite news |title=Bill Brooks signs with Bills |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/rushville-republican-bill-brooks-signs-w/146383769/ |access-date=April 30, 2024 |work=Rushville Republican |agency=Associated Press |date=April 2, 1993}}</ref>

Brooks was the Colts' leading receiver for five of his seven seasons with the team. When he left the Colts, Brooks was ranked second all-time in receptions and fourth all-time in franchise receiving yards. As of the 2023 NFL season, Brooks is ranked seventh on the [[List of Indianapolis Colts records#Career leaders|Colts all-time receiving yards list]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Indianapolis Colts Career Receiving Leaders |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/clt/career-receiving.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref>

Brooks later became the first Indianapolis Colts player to be inducted into the [[Indianapolis Colts Ring of Honor]] on August 22, 1998.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://bonesaw.tripod.com/records5.htm# | title=Colts Records, Page 5}}</ref>

===Buffalo Bills (1993–1995)===
Brooks joined a Bills team that had won three consecutive [[AFC Championships]] from 1990-1992. Brooks replaced retired [[Starting lineup|starter]] [[James Lofton]] and quickly made a connection with star quarterback [[Jim Kelly]]. Brooks, [[Pro Bowl]] receiver [[Andre Reed]], and [[tight end]] [[Pete Metzelaars]] were Kelly's primary targets on the season.<ref>{{cite news |title=Brooks a 'Family Man' |url=https://www.sun-sentinel.com/1994/01/16/brooks-a-family-man/ |access-date=April 30, 2024 |work=South Florida Sun Sentinel |date=January 16, 1994}}</ref> Brooks saw a return to form, with 60 receptions for 714 yards and five touchdowns on the season.<ref name=PFR /> The Bills continued to dominate the AFC, going 12-4 on the regular season and again winning the conference. In the [[NFL playoffs, 1993-94#AFC: Buffalo Bills 29.2C Los Angeles Raiders 23|1993-94 NFL Playoffs Divisional Round]], Brooks caught six passes for 92 yards and two touchdowns in the Bills 29–23 win over the [[Oakland Raiders|Los Angeles Raiders]], including the game-sealing touchdown in the fourth quarter.<ref>{{cite web |title=Divisional Round - Los Angeles Raiders at Buffalo Bills - January 15th, 1994 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199401150buf.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref> In [[Super Bowl XXVIII]], the Bills saw their fourth straight Super Bowl defeat, losing 13-30 to the [[Dallas Cowboys]].<ref>{{cite web |title=1993 Buffalo Bills Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/buf/1993.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref> Brooks had seven receptions for 63 yards in Super Bowl XXVIII.<ref>{{cite web |title=Super Bowl XXVIII - Dallas Cowboys vs. Buffalo Bills - January 30th, 1994 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199401300buf.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref>

The 1994 season was a down year for the Bills and Brooks. Coming off of four straight Super Bowl appearances, the Bills finished the season at a disappointing 7-9.<ref>{{cite web |title=1994 Buffalo Bills Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/buf/1994.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref> Reed continued to shine, garnering most of the team's receptions with over 1,300 receiving yards on the season. Brooks started in nine games, recording 42 receptions for 482 yards and two touchdowns.<ref name=PFR />

In 1995, Brooks and the Bills had a return to form. Reed was injured for much of the year, providing Brooks with more playing opportunities. Brooks took advantage of his expanded role and caught 53 passes for 763 yards and a career-high 11 touchdowns.<ref name=PFR /> The Bills went 10-6 on the season, winning the AFC East and making the playoffs. Brooks had three games in the regular season where he recorded at least 100 receiving yards and two touchdowns.<ref>{{cite web |title=1995 Buffalo Bills Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/buf/1995.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref> In the [[1995-96 NFL playoffs]], the Bills defeated the [[Miami Dolphins]] in the Wild Card round 37-22 before losing to the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] in the Divisional Round.

Brooks left the Bills after the 1995 season as an unrestricted free agent.

===Washington Redskins (1996)===
On May 9, 1996, Brooks signed a one-year contract with the [[Washington Redskins]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sell |first1=Dave |title=Redskins pick up receiver |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1996/05/11/redskins-pick-up-receiver/404f5872-f092-4954-9325-3a3da716de00/ |access-date=April 30, 2024 |work=The Washington Post |date=May 10, 1996}}</ref> Brooks was signed as a veteran presence and his playing time was limited. Brooks recorded two starts in the 1996 season for Washington, ending the season with 17 receptions for 224 yards.<ref name=PFR />

Brooks finished his 11-year NFL career with 583 receptions for 8,001 yards and 46 touchdowns. He also recorded 18 rushing attempts for 106 yards.<ref name=PFR />

==Post-playing career and personal life==
In 1998, Brooks rejoined the Indianapolis Colts as the Director of Community Development/Player Relations.<ref>{{cite web |title=Indianapolis Colts 1998 Media Guide |url=https://res.cloudinary.com/nflclubs/image/upload/colts/apseqdtgj7urwtk1twbd.pdf |page=2 |website=Colts.com |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref> Brooks' family had remained in Indianapolis while he played in Buffalo and Washington. In 2002, Brooks was promoted by the Colts to Executive Director of Administration, serving in that role from 2002 to 2009.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.colts.com/sub.cfm?page%3Dinformation_dynamic%26id%3D89 |title=The Official Website of the Indianapolis Colts |accessdate=May 31, 2007 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070313001102/http://www.colts.com/sub.cfm?page=information_dynamic&id=89 |archivedate=March 13, 2007 }}</ref> In 2020, Brooks returned to the Indianapolis Colts as the Team Ambassador, appearing on Colts radio and podcast programs.<ref name=JJ />

Brooks is active in community projects, especially in his adopted hometown of [[Indianapolis]]. Brooks received the Sagamore of the Wabash by Indiana Governor [[Evan Bayh]] in 1990. From 1991-1992, he served as the Indianapolis Colts' United Way spokesman. In 1996, he received the [[Byron "Whizzer" White NFL Man of the Year Award]] for community impact. Brooks received several Indianapolis-based community leadership awards and has served on several non-profit boards. Brooks earned a Master's in Business Administration degree from [[Butler University]] while a member of the Colts.<ref>{{cite web |title=2003 Indianapolis Colts Media Guide |url=https://static.clubs.nfl.com/image/upload/colts/vbzepvnqezdkrkudbdmg.pdf |website=Colts.com |access-date=April 30, 2024}}</ref>

'''William Joseph Adams''' (born February 4, 1950) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Guard (American football)|guard]] for six seasons with the [[Buffalo Bills]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He later became a longtime high school football coach and athletic director in Massachusetts.

Adams played [[college football]] for the [[Holy Cross Crusaders football|Holy Cross Crusaders]], with whom he was a standout offensive guard. He was selected by the [[Miami Dolphins]] in the [[1972 NFL draft]] but played his entire NFL career with the [[Buffalo Bills]], where he was part of the famed “Electric Company” offensive line that blocked for [[O. J. Simpson]] during his 2,000-yard rushing season. After retiring from professional football, Adams worked for over 30 years in education and coaching, including nearly two decades as head coach at [[Lynnfield High School]].

== Early life and college ==
Adams was born in [[Lynn, Massachusetts]], and raised in nearby [[Swampscott, Massachusetts|Swampscott]]. He attended [[Swampscott High School]], where he starred as an offensive lineman under coach Stan Bondelevitch. Adams was named an All-Scholastic player and participated in the Agganis All-Star Game after his senior year.

He went on to play at the [[College of the Holy Cross]], where he transitioned from linebacker to offensive guard. Adams was named first-team All-New England and received the Davitt Award as the [[Holy Cross Crusaders football|Crusaders]]' top offensive lineman.

== Professional career ==
Adams was selected in the seventh round (161st overall) of the [[1972 NFL draft]] by the [[Miami Dolphins]], but was released before the season. He was signed by the [[Buffalo Bills]] shortly thereafter and remained with the team through the 1978 season.

Adams played in 46 career games, starting one. Though primarily a backup, he was part of the offensive line known as the "Electric Company," which helped [[O. J. Simpson]] rush for over 2,000 yards in 1973. He played behind All-Pro guards [[Joe DeLamielleure]] and [[Reggie McKenzie (guard)|Reggie McKenzie]].

He retired from the NFL in 1979 at age 29, choosing to focus on family and life beyond football.

== Coaching and teaching career ==
Following his NFL career, Adams became a teacher and coach at [[Lynnfield High School]] in Massachusetts. He served as head football coach from the late 1980s to 2007, leading the team to several winning seasons, including a 9–1 record in 1991. He also coached basketball and served as the school’s athletic director beginning in 1994.

He was inducted into the [[Massachusetts High School Football Coaches Association]] Hall of Fame for his long-standing contributions to high school sports.

== Personal life ==
Adams continued working in education after his retirement from full-time teaching, serving as a substitute teacher and interim athletic director at nearby high schools. He resides in Massachusetts.

'''Anthony Bernard Scott''' (born February 10, 1984) is an American former professional [[Gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] in the sixth round of the [[2009 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Abilene Christian Wildcats football|Abilene Christian Wildcats]]. His brother [[Daryl Richardson]] is also a former NFL running back.

==Early life==
A native of [[Vernon, Texas]], Scott had a troubled past.<ref name="troubled">{{cite news |url=http://www.wnewsj.com/main.asp?SectionID=1&SubSectionID=1&ArticleID=176222&TM=55194.8 |title=Bengals take a chance on troubled RB Scott |newspaper=Wilmington News Journal |date=April 27, 2009 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110719082020/http://www.wnewsj.com/main.asp?SectionID=1&SubSectionID=1&ArticleID=176222&TM=55194.8 |archivedate=July 19, 2011 }}</ref> A Class 3A first-team all-state selection as a high school junior in 2001, Scott was kicked off his high school team at [[Vernon High School (Texas)|Vernon High School]] because of an off-campus fight after the season.<ref name="troubled" /> He was not eligible for his senior year, and finally graduated from [[Wichita Falls High School]] in 2003.

==College career==
He went on to attend [[Central Arkansas University]], where he earned [[Gulf South Conference]] Freshman of the Year honors in 2004, but was eventually dismissed from the football team for hitting a coach, along with a few other issues.<ref name="troubled" /> Scott transferred to [[Blinn College]], where he was a first-team [[National Junior College Athletic Association|NJCAA]] All-America after leading the Buccaneers to a 12–0 season and the NJCAA national championship. Scott averaged 154.4 rushing yards per game, and he finished his only junior college season with a junior college-best 1,892 yards and 27 touchdowns. He was also first-team all Southwestern Junior College Football Conference.

Rated a three-star recruit by ''[[Rivals.com]]'', Scott drew some interest by [[University of Arkansas|Arkansas]] and [[Fresno State University|Fresno State]],<ref>{{Citation |title=Bernard Scott Recruiting Profile |work=Rivals.com |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/ncaa/football/recruiting/player-Bernard-Scott-56863 }}</ref> but eventually enrolled at [[Abilene Christian University]] in 2007. He had finished runner-up in the voting for the 2007 [[Harlon Hill Trophy]] to [[Danny Woodhead]]. In that year, Scott broke the league's single-season rushing record with 2,165 yards and set a pair of NCAA Division II single-season records with 39 total touchdowns and 234 points scored.<ref name="Richards">{{cite news |first=Joey |last=Richards |title=ACU coach staying; star back signs with agent |url=http://www.reporternews.com/news/2008/dec/19/acu-coach-staying-star-back-signs-with-agent/ |work=[[Abilene Reporter-News]] |date=December 19, 2008 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090418161125/http://www.reporternews.com/news/2008/dec/19/acu-coach-staying-star-back-signs-with-agent/ |archivedate=April 18, 2009 }}</ref> In 2008, Scott won the Harlon Hill Trophy in a landslide, getting the third-highest vote total in the 23-year history of the trophy.

==Professional career==

===Pre-draft===
Scott's NFL prospects were tarnished by his off-the-field issues. Besides his aforementioned trouble in high school and junior college, he was also arrested for some traffic-related misdemeanors, and was put on an 18-month probation for failing to identify himself during a traffic stop in [[Abilene, Texas|Abilene]] in the spring of 2007.<ref name="Richards" />

===Cincinnati Bengals===
Scott was selected 209th overall by the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] in the sixth round of the 2009 NFL Draft.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2009 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2009/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-13 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

Following training camp, Scott made the active roster as a kick returner and as a backup to running back [[Cedric Benson]]. On November 15, 2009, Scott returned a kickoff 96 yards for a touchdown against the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]], which earned him AFC Special Teams Player of the Week honors.<ref>{{Citation |url=http://news.cincinnati.com/article/20091118/SPT02/311180086 |last1=Reedy |first1=Joe |last2=Erardi |first2=John |title=Rookie Bernard Scott honored by AFC |newspaper=Cincinnati Enquirer |date=November 18, 2009 }}</ref>

In his first career start, in week 11 against the [[Oakland Raiders]], Scott rushed for 119 yards, including a 61-yard run that was the longest by a Bengal since [[Corey Dillon]]'s 67-yard rush at [[Cleveland Browns|Cleveland]] on September 15, 2002.<ref>{{Citation |url=http://www.bengals.com/news/article-1/Bengals-Raided-in-clutch/ef2a5008-5ff2-470e-9d92-20821c480f85 |title=Bengals Raided in clutch |last=Hobson |first=Geoff |date=November 23, 2009 |work=Bengals.com |access-date=November 23, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091125022448/http://www.bengals.com/news/article-1/Bengals-Raided-in-clutch/ef2a5008-5ff2-470e-9d92-20821c480f85 |archive-date=November 25, 2009 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He also became the first Bengals rookie to rush for 100 yards in a game since Dillon in {{NFL Year|1997}}.

===Baltimore Ravens===
Scott signed with the [[Baltimore Ravens]] on October 28, 2013. On December 7, 2013, the Ravens released Scott.<ref>[https://twitter.com/Ravens/status/409431946633437185 Twitter / Ravens: #Ravens waived RB Bernard Scott to make room for TE Dennis Pitta on the roster.]</ref> On December 10, after a season-ending injury to [[Brandon Stokley]], Scott re-signed with the Ravens.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.baltimoreravens.com/news/article-1/Brandon-Stokley-Placed-On-Injured-Reserve/166d845e-7512-4ff9-a66f-259b14beb2eb |title=Brandon Stokley Placed On Injured Reserve |access-date=December 10, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131212105231/http://www.baltimoreravens.com/news/article-1/Brandon-Stokley-Placed-On-Injured-Reserve/166d845e-7512-4ff9-a66f-259b14beb2eb |archive-date=December 12, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===Toronto Argonauts===
On March 3, 2015, Scott signed with the [[Toronto Argonauts]] of the [[Canadian Football League]]. He retired in May 2015.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cfl.ca/article/argos-rb-steve-slaton-retires-from-football |title=Argos RBs Slaton, Scott announce retirement |publisher=cfl.ca |date=May 21, 2015 |accessdate=May 22, 2015 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150522200431/http://www.cfl.ca/article/argos-rb-steve-slaton-retires-from-football |archivedate=May 22, 2015 }}</ref>

'''William Berry Acker Jr.''' (born November 7, 1956) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive tackle]] for six seasons for the [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]], [[Kansas City Chiefs]], and [[Buffalo Bills]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Texas Longhorns football|Texas Longhorns]]. 

==College career==
Acker played college football at [[The University of Texas]] between 1975 and 1979, but missed the 1976 season. In 1975, he helped the Longhorns win a share of the Southwest Conference Championship and defeat Colorado in the [[1975 Astro-Bluebonnet Bowl]] to finish ranked #6/#7. In 1977, he helped the Longhorns win the Southwest Conference Championship, spend the last 6 weeks of the season ranked #1 and play for the National Championship in the [[1978 Cotton Bowl Classic]] which they lost to Notre Dame. He helped the team win the [[1978 Sun Bowl]] and finish ranked #9 while he was named Second-team ([[1978 All-Southwest Conference football team|All-Southwest Conference]]. That season he tied the then-school record for sacks in a season with 14 and led the team in forced fumbles.<ref name="Record">{{cite web |title=Texas Football Record Book |url=https://texaslonghorns.com/documents/2024/8/8/Football_Record_Book.pdf |access-date=14 February 2025}}</ref> He captained the 1979 team that finished the season ranked #12/#13 after losing the [[1979 Sun Bowl]] to [[1979 Washington Huskies football team|Washington]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Texas Football History Honors |url=https://texaslonghorns.com/documents/2024/8/8/Football_History___Honors.pdf |access-date=14 February 2025}}</ref>

In the four seasons he played for Texas, the Longhorns were never unranked. Acker left the school having gotten more sacks in his career than any other Longhorn prior to him and topped only by teammate Tim Campbell. He also had the 2nd most forced fumbles.<ref name="Record"/>

==Professional career==
Acker was selected by the Cardinals in the sixth round of the [[1980 NFL draft]], #142 overall.

==Personal life==
His brother [[Jim Acker|Jim]] is a former [[MLB]] pitcher.<ref>{{cite news|title=1987 Topps baseball card # 407}}</ref>

'''William Arthur Belk''' (born February 19, 1946) is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] [[Lineman (gridiron football)#Defensive line|defensive lineman]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[San Francisco 49ers]] in the sixth round of the [[1968 NFL/AFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] at [[University of Maryland Eastern Shore|Maryland Eastern Shore]].  He played for the [[Toronto Argonauts]] in the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL) in 1975 and 1976. He played a total of 9 years of professional football.

Belk was inducted into the University of Maryland Eastern-Shore Hall of Fame in 1984. His collegiate career spanned from 1964 to 1968. In college, Belk was a two-way starter at
offensive and defensive end. He received All-Conference honors in 1966 and 1967, and was co-captain of the team his senior year. While in college, Belk was a student athlete, making the honor roll and dean’s list. He graduated in 1968, earning a bachelor's degree in Business Education.

In the NFL, Belk proved to be a versatile, reliable, and very intelligent football player, starting at both defensive end and tackle. One of his coaches, Dick Nolan, made this testimony in reference to Belk, “What I like about Bill is that he's very smart. He knows exactly what he's doing out there and can adjust to any situation."

== Professional career ==

=== San Francisco 49ers (1968–1974) ===
Belk made an impact in his rookie season when he stepped up for [[Kevin Hardy (defensive tackle)|Kevin Hardy]] after he went down with a right knee sprain.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Church |first=Jim |date=November 18, 1968 |title=Not hurt by 49er tie - Allen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YmNLAAAAIBAJ&dq=bill+belk+%22football%22&pg=PA6 |access-date=December 13, 2024 |work=The Press-Courier |pages=11}}</ref> By his third season with the team, despite suffering some injuries early in his career, he was seen as an integral part of the team, coming off the bench.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Timms |first=Leslie |date=October 8, 1970 |title=Belk wants starting job |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MoIsAAAAIBAJ&dq=bill+belk+%22football%22&pg=PA17 |access-date=December 13, 2024 |work=Herald-Journal}}</ref> In 1975, he was waived by the 49ers.<ref>{{Cite news |date=September 11, 1975 |title=Pros trim again |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZF4sAAAAIBAJ&dq=bill+belk+%22football%22&pg=PA16 |access-date=December 13, 2024 |work=Herald-Journal}}</ref>

=== Toronto Argonauts ===
In 1975, Belk joined the [[Toronto Argonauts]] in the [[Canadian Football League]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=October 2, 1975 |title=Argonauts pose test for Bomber running |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MT5VAAAAIBAJ&dq=bill+belk+%22football%22&pg=PA17 |access-date=December 13, 2024 |work=[[The Leader-Post]]}}</ref>
